120.t: Being remembered for Condon's records around the world
120.s: Fans in Europe and everywhere thank him for the Condon records, which have been reissued, and he says whether it was a peak is a matter of taste.
120.q: And, today, when I play Europe and you know, I play all over the world now, I never play a place that guys don't come and say - well, thank you for Eddie Condon's and we've started our band from your style-- of records and--- to this day and this is thirty someting years later, they have never…

120.t: Treated as an artist in Europe, forgotten at home
120.s: Europe paid better and respected him; he blames American television and radio and rock money for dropping his kind of jazz.
120.q: But the point is that - how I was treated after I got there and the money was so much better and I was treated like I was - instead of just another jazz musician, I was treated like an artist.

120.t: First job in Denmark and a new life
120.s: His first Danish job was a youth centre where people danced to his kind of music; tours are extended and he makes dozens of albums and a television life story.
120.q: Yeah - well for posterity -- good God - I'm not dead yet. But, the point is that when I went to Denmark, I got a shock of my life -- the first

120.t: Countries played and recorded in
120.s: He reads off the countries he has played, from Austria to Argentina, recording in almost all of them.
120.q: You couldn't do it here - nobody was interested. But, over there, they were. And, so, now as I go along on these five years scene and I'm staying and I wanted to stay more and more and the longer I stayed the more work I got; I actually got to the point in Europe where I was turning down jobs; I…

120.t: Aarhus, the Pa Pa Bue Viking Jazz Band and changing its style
120.s: He plays first in Aarhus, with Fessor's Big City Band, then joins Pa Pa Bue's band for nearly a year and gets them playing his melodic swing way.
120.q: They must have ten good jazz bands in that town but I played my first four or five days in Denmark there and uh, and back

120.t: The European festival circuit and its value to musicians
120.s: Festivals in Holland, Germany, England, Nice and Berne, which he helped start, give American musicians steady work.
120.q: Something around in there - yeah - and, then, there was another--- well, I want to mention too that these festivals in Europe - like in Holland and there are German festivals; there's English festivals now-- and it certainly had done great by American musicians and there's the one in France---

120.t: The doctors' band Swing Four Seven and the Louis Armstrong imitator Theis Nyegaard
120.s: A band of Danish doctors with a dentist arranger swings like 52nd Street and gave him a televised farewell party; another leader plays only Armstrong's repertoire.
120.q: of tapes with them; and, I did a couple of television shows. They call themselves "Swing Four Seven" and they've got the most fantastic rhythm section I ever heard. They have a dentist - my dentist by the way - who plays tenor saxophone, clarinet and alto and writes for this band and I want to tell…

120.t: Touring Switzerland and meeting Hans Zurbrugg's Wolverines at Nice
120.s: After a cultural tour twenty years earlier, he is booked by George Wein with a Swiss Dixieland band at Nice and fits in without asking them to learn his songs.
120.q: first time I had ever seen Switzerland, but this time - when I went back - I had played for George Wein in Nice and, of course, George always puts things on the bulletin board everyday where you're suppose to appear and the second thing I did in that-- of that particular day, I think it was the…

120.t: How the Berne festival began in a hotel room
120.s: The Swiss band invites him for a tour and then a small festival; he phones Cliff Leeman and Ralph Sutton to bring the rest of the Condon band, all expenses paid.
120.q: Yes, which I've been doing all my life - that kind of stuff - but they didn't know that. So, they were very impressed and I made very good friends with all these guys. Marvelous band. So, they invited me to Switzerland and I went and did a tour with them before they had--- I did just a small tour…

120.t: This year's Berne lineup with Peanuts Hucko and the radio big band
120.s: He plans two Dixieland swing bands, Kenny Davern and Pee Wee Erwin, and Peanuts Hucko with the Swiss radio band playing Glenn Miller arrangements.
120.q: Well, this year, I'm going to have all the ones left in the Condon band-- I've got all of them and I've got one other whole American band---

120.t: The Dutch Swing College Band and recordings with Ted Easton
120.s: He does forty one-nighters in Germany with the highly professional Dutch band, then records in Holland and with another Dutch leader.
120.q: have Peanuts for one of the concerts as well with us, which will make it all - just one whole band - all of the old Condon guys - different guys that played with the Condon group. And, then, of course, I started going through Holland; in Holland I did several concerts in Europe in Germany as well,…

120.t: Ann runs the logistics and a Swedish tour
120.s: Ann maps out his dates; he tours Sweden by a 35-minute crossing from Denmark, last playing with a band called Kris Bandits.
120.q: So, uh, it was--- it was a job for my wife to keep this thing going and mapping it out, where I'm going to be and so on. How long it takes to get there--

120.t: Germany: the Flat Foot Stompers and good money
120.s: He plays with the Flat Foot Stompers and the Barrelhouse Jazz Band and records with them; Germany pays the most and answers quickly.
120.q: -- I've been with many, many bands in Germany. The last time I was in Germany, I played near Stuttgart-- and to show you the interest now about what's happening, in a place like Germany - Germany is one of the best buying countries of jazz in the world right today - they've got the money - believe…

120.t: England has the best audience in the world
120.s: Visiting yearly since about 1965, he says English listeners come to listen, throw out noisy people and follow him year after year.
120.q: Well, I think actually - to tell you the truth, I think I'm better known in England than I am in America. I really mean it; Just that every place I go to it's sort of a fan thing for me. I stay at peoples houses and they're just--- I think-- I can safely say that I think the American-- the English…

120.t: English bands and thirty-one bands in thirty days
120.s: He names Alex Welsh's old players, Humphrey Lyttelton and others, and says on his last tour he played with thirty-one different bands.
120.q: Oh, England--- Well, of course, England is loaded - just loaded with great musicians. And, all those old members of the Alex Welsh Band are now world famous and, of course, it was very unfortunate that the band broke up, but they all gone with the other great bands in England; there's about ten…

120.t: The Pizza Express Jazz Club in London
120.s: He describes the downstairs club where a different band plays each night and backs visiting Americans.
120.q: No - it's a fantastic restaurant -- upstairs -- it's a downstairs place and upstairs they --- you can have any kind of pizza you ever heard of in your

120.t: Austria's Jazz Land tunnel and Brussels
120.s: A band plays in a tunnel under a thousand-year-old Vienna church; the one good Brussels club is packed but noisy.
120.q: And, when the Turks had taken over that country, they had-- they made this tunnel underneath the city so they could feed the people inside -- The Turks had surrounded the city and had it locked up, and they turned that into a jazz club and this guy calls it his band - it's a steady band - he calls…

120.t: Czechoslovakia and the Jazz Collegium Whiteman copy
120.s: Behind the Iron Curtain he records with a band that reproduces Paul Whiteman's arrangements, taking Bix's solos, in a country where jazz was once smuggled.
120.q: Yes and, uh, when you go to a place like that, you wonder what the hell you're getting into -- and, of course, in Czechoslovakia, I ran into a band called the Jazz Collegium - whatever they call themselves---

120.t: Poland's jazz competition and the young trumpeter
120.s: He plays and then judges a week-long Warsaw competition, impressed by a band whose trumpeter hits notes only dogs could hear.
120.q: Yeah - and then, of course you know I played Poland and I loved the band in Poland - I went there to play a thing called the, uh, jazz party of some kind and it's a competition thing - they have hundreds of Polish bands - you wouldn't believe it - for seven days - hundreds of them just appearing…

120.t: European jazz is high in quality and sincere
120.s: European musicians play only American songs with real interest; Czech songs sounded American, and the first they asked him to learn was I'll Build a Fence Around You.
120.q: Yes, it is and the biggest thing I want to put across is this -- their interest. They are so sincere with their playing, you know -- it's-- they shoes --old button shoes don't feel - well, it's not old / to them - they're really working at it.

120.t: Italy with Lino Patruno, Monte Carlo, Norway and Scotland
120.s: He plays with a television-star guitarist in Italy, Monte Carlo for IBM, Norway and Scotland, finding bands that play his style except one two-beat group.
120.q: I call him Lini Patrinì but that's the best I can do -- but anyway, here again, I ran into a hell of a band; I've recorded with them twice; made a long playing album and, uh, he is a T.V. star; he is a comedian, a T.V. star; he is a movie star; he is the best guitar player--- one of the best guitar…

120.t: How he was invited to Argentina
120.s: Two Argentine fans hear him in Copenhagen, listen to tapes at his house and arrange contracts; a Buenos Aires band sounds like Condon's.
120.q: Airlines and he had a friend with him called Tito and they claimed that they came-- that they had been listening to my records in Buenos Aires for a year and they wanted to come and hear me personally - they heard I was there; one guy was 2,000 miles from there; he flew in just to get there for…

120.t: The Buenos Aires press conference and warm reception
120.s: He is put up in a suite, faces fifty reporters through an interpreter, and is hailed by trumpeters as their teacher.
120.q: Oh, well, I'm getting to that -- that was in the hotel I'm talking about -- they put us up in this great hotel and they had a suite of rooms with two televisions -- one in one room and one in the other and all this -- I even said to them - You certainly don't have to have a suite of rooms for me --…

120.t: Using Denmark as a landing field
120.s: Denmark has jazz festivals, and he lives there as a base from which to fly to jobs across Europe.
120.q: On the ensembles I'd play the second part which makes the band sound very big-- now, these are just some of the bands that are in Denmark; Denmark

120.t: Hungary and Ireland
120.s: Hungary is relaxed with little sign of communism; in Northern Ireland he finds a fine Irish band.
120.q: Yeah, and of course, I played in Hungary. Now, Hungary is--- there's no way - there's no sign of Communists there only that some of the buildings have red stars on them, but you don't see any of the people - soldiers and such in the streets and you're free to buy there; you can buy anything you…

120.t: Leaving when Condon moved uptown, and tours of Germany and England
120.s: When the downtown club closed he declined the uptown place and accepted his first European tour on his own, then an Alex Welsh tour.
120.q: Well, it came to an end -- when the downtown closed that's when I decided that I didn't want to go to the uptown place. And, I had--- now, this is long after our tour---

120.t: The Danish Radio Big Band and state-funded jazz
120.s: He praises the radio big band with strings and woodwind doublers, Niels-Henning bassist and Thad Jones as leader; government radio pays, and Denmark has ninety jazz clubs.
120.q: Oh - I work as much as I like in Denmark; as I said before, it's the only place where I've ever been where I really had to turn down work. You know--they've got probably one of the best big bands in Europe that works through the radio -- they call it the radio big band -- they use four trombones,…

120.t: Stuyvesant Casino weekends and the disastrous 1957 England tour with Condon
120.s: Beside record dates he picks up weekend money, then tours England with the Condon band, where Condon's drinking and an insult to a society editor ruin the visit.
120.q: - one of the many, many things we did out of Condon's - of course - we did piles of record dates, as you know and, uh, I was working Fridays and Saturdays - I went and stopped by Bob Mall's place - you know, the place - over on the Third Avenue, the Stuyvesant Casino, and I'd pick up a couple of…

112.t: German audiences expect Africans
112.s: Audiences expected savages and could not believe the band were Americans; they gave seventy sold-out performances.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: It was something new and it was something like that occasion in Copenhagen that happened. Some of them were waiting to see gorillas and baboons and everything. They didn't know what they were going to see. Well, when these guys come at that time, because they didn't -- they didn't see no bad…

112.t: After the opening: Berlin night out and sightseeing
112.s: Wooding declines a Berlin brothel visit because his wife is along, then tours the Kaiser's palace and coffee-houses with big bands.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: person anyhow. Anyhow, so then we went out. Now we went to -- right away the Germans said, "Well we must take you first to a bawdy house." We went to this bawdy house. But here's what I didn't need. I'd been always respected by Lyons and all of them and I had my wife with me, so, as well as I…

112.t: German musicians, improvisation and syncopating Wagner
112.s: German musicians could not follow improvisation, and the band syncopated Tannhauser, which some called sacrilege.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: Oh, yeah. Yeah, they come up and they couldn't understand it. They couldn't understand what we were doing and why we were doing it. And they didn't know anything about improvising. They were good musicians but they didn't know -- well I'd take a piece, and after the guy's been playing for awhile, I…

112.t: Copenhagen success, expulsion and the orangutan review
112.s: Copenhagen was the greatest success after Berlin, but authorities put them out for taking all the money, and a newspaper called Wooding an orangutan.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: Now, but we were a big success. But our greatest success after Berlin was Copenhagen. And that's where we saw the girls before the show, when we came in there, the sophisticated women sitting there with the cigars, you know, the small cigars? And so we used to call them the Great Danes.

112.t: European musicians try to copy the band
112.s: At the Fawn des Westen in Berlin a German band attempts improvisation and the master of ceremonies tells the audience to applaud them.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: We had a band, after, when we come out of Russia, we went to a place called Fawn Des Westen in Berlin. And again we played and there was a German band on the stand, so that they had an idea that we might do something like this, too. Their improvisation was like cacophony. And they were mixed up.…

112.t: English audiences and attitudes
112.s: English audiences were fine but cooler than German and Danish ones, he says, and acted like an older brother toward America.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: Yes, they were. They were. But England didn't appeal to people so much as it did on the continent, because, outside of the hotels the living wasn't so good.

112.t: Friendships and sex in Europe
112.s: He says they seldom befriended European artists and musicians and instead enjoyed freedom to mix with white women in Europe.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: : Well that was hard -- Chris, that was funny. You know, we were young and we were exposed to something that we wasn't exposed to in America. And that was the association, and cohabiting... (unintelligible). Well Chris, I'll tell you this much. We would meet some artists some times. But not so…

112.t: First concert by a Black band in Copenhagen
112.s: The Chocolate Kiddies Orchestra gives its own concert in February 1931 at the Odd Fellow Palais and then about ten others.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: : Yeah. And so, from then, after we finished Valencia, that's we -- where we try giving our first concert. Black concert.

112.t: Politiken Christmas concert and how far Black Americans have come
112.s: He recalls sharing a bill with the Danish Symphony and says Europe gave freedom, while America now has Black mayors.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: Yes. I had a couple of writeups also from the symphony orchestra leader in Berlin, too, and the one in Copenhagen. But I lost them. I would have liked to have them, but I lost them.

112.t: Going home so his child would be born American
112.s: With his wife pregnant and citizenship in doubt, he decides to go home at Christmas 1931.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: We was in France at the time, and there was this thing there that unless you declared the child, declared it before it was 18 or something, it would be a citizen of that country. And I didn't want no bother like that, so there wasn't nothing else for me to do. Mother was getting older, so I…

112.t: Nazi pressure voids his Haus Germania contract
112.s: He explains that his Berlin birthday-gift contract was barred because the rising Nazi Party did not want American or Black music.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: Europe had sort of lost the spark. And what made me lose the spark was, when I was in the (HAUS GERMANIA), the year before, for my birthday, which was in June, the fellow gave me three months to return to the following year, next year. To come back there, that was my birthday present, see? And the…

112.t: Ufa Palast, the rise of Hitler and a tour to Vienna
112.s: After six weeks at the Ufa Palast and Hamburg, the band tours Spain, Italy and Vienna; he saw Nazi organizing already.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: Oh yes. That's the reason they sent for us. They had this Ernie Rappe there, an American. Because things were down there, you know, in those days it wasn't so good either. Germany needed a shot in the arm. And they began to get it through the organization, that was looking Hitler, began raising his…

112.t: Arthur Lyons leaves for Hollywood; Spadoni sends him back to Europe
112.s: Lyons hands his business to his brother and goes to Hollywood, and Wooding returns to Europe under Spadoni through Eddie Duisberg.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: For the vaudeville there. And then he turned his business over to -- in '27 or the early part of '28, over to his brother Sam Lyons. And he went to, went out to Hollywood, because everything was moving out that way. And Arthur was really up on the ball. I think he ended up by being the manager for…

112.t: London Savoy contract cancelled
112.s: The Savoy booking collapsed after American bands barred Jack Hylton, so he returned home.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: No. Now the six months in the Savoy in London. That was rescinded because Paul Whiteman and Paul Specht and some of the white bands, had refused Jack Hilton's entry into America. Jack Hilton had a much (staged) band that was much better than Paul Whiteman or any of the American stage bands. He had…

112.t: Glad to forget hardships at home
112.s: Asked about keeping up with America, he says he was happy to be out of the hardships of his homeland.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: You see. And some of the hardships and all that we had, we were happy to say we were out of it. And at one time --

112.t: Jazz treatments of Tannhauser and the 1812 Overture
112.s: He describes the band's modern versions of Wagner and Rimsky-Korsakov and a bells-and-cannon 1812 Overture.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: Like, (sings Tannhauser). But at the same time, we would be using, (sings syncopated accompaniment). Things like that, with the saxophone. And it turned out well. Well, we had quite a number of them that we did. Some Rimsky-Korsakov, and one that we had was the "Overture of 1812". And we had it…

112.t: Germans astonished by Black Americans; the Gene Cedric incident
112.s: At the Darmstader Hoff, Gene Cedric scares an inquisitive German woman reading his letter, and Wooding reflects that Germans thought Africans were brought to America temporarily.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: Now we was all staying at -- we lived at a place called Darmstader Hoff. This all happened in East Berlin, on Friederich-strasse. And as we were standing outside talking, one of the boys, Gene Cedric -- he was tenor saxophone, later on became very popular over here with Fats Waller and some other…

112.t: Stockholm and a benefit for Prince Carl
112.s: In Stockholm he does a Red Cross benefit for Prince Carl of Sweden.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: And we had a great benefit. That was in the Haselbach, it was a great hall there. But the band played, I mean the show was in a place something like the Tivoli would be in Copenhagen.

112.t: Arthur Lyons brings in a European impresario
112.s: Lyons introduces the Russian impresario Lenidow, who wants a band and a show, and cast members for Europe are found.
112.ch: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
112.q: And then one day Lyons come in and said to me, "How would you like to go to Europe?" I looked at him as if to say, "Are you kidding?" He said no, I've got a man, an impresario from Europe. A man named Leonidoff. Not the one in Radio City. This was, he spelled his name -L-e-n-i-d-o-w, which is the…

112.t: Signing the Europe contract and the voyage over
112.s: The contract was signed at four in the morning in early 1925 and the band, with wives and friends, had a carefree crossing in summer.
112.ch: Chocolate Kiddies in Europe
112.q: Yeah. See, because we went over in that July, or that August, see. And opened up in Berlin in either August or September.

112.t: Madrid, the royal visit, bullfights and Moorish-flavoured music
112.s: In Madrid they restart the show for the Spanish royals, learn the anthem, and hear Catalonian music he links to the Moors.
112.ch: South America and back in New York
112.q: And also, that was our first chance to see a bullfight. And listen to the music of Catalonia. They had the music, in fact, even the instruments were original. This music was the wildest thing. I think it was part Moorish music. It was the

611.t: Audiences in Czechoslovakia, Poland and France
611.s: He found the best audiences in Czechoslovakia and Poland, dressed in tuxedos and listening in silence.
611.q: Well I don’t know. That’s really a good question. That has been asked me so often. If you want to know where I think are the greatest audiences that I’ve ever played for, it was not in Europe and not in America either, it was in the what do you call it, Czechoslovakia and Poland. That’s where the…

611.t: Going to Europe with Archey, December 1952
611.s: After about three years at Ryan's, Waters sailed with Archey's band for a month's European tour just before Christmas, thinking of Paris.
611.q: Yeah, and I went there in 1950, the end of 1950, the end of December.

611.t: Hamburg, Switzerland and the Archey band breaking up
611.s: The tour went to Hamburg then Switzerland, where the band broke up after Archey joined Earl Hines in San Francisco; Waters forfeited his return ticket and stayed with Bill Coleman.
611.q: Hamburg - we started in Hamburg and played a week or somethin' like that in Hamburg. And then we looked for Hamburg - Switzerland - and the band broke up in Switzerland.

611.t: Replacing Dicky Wells in Bill Coleman's band
611.s: Coleman's group worked clubs in Switzerland and Germany, but Dicky Wells and Zutty Singleton had tired of it. Waters accepted Coleman's offer, hoping the band would reach Paris.
611.q: Well, Dicky Wells was working with Bill Coleman at the point. And Bill was doing the, working [ ] clubs, you know - club dates, see, weekend, weekday, like that, see. And some of them Germany also. And Bill was from Paris, too, he live in Paris.

611.t: Forming a Paris band with Bill Coleman
611.s: With Zutty and the pianist gone, Waters and Coleman rehearsed a new band of French and Martinique musicians in Paris for a French tour.
611.q: No, no, not that great, see. So anyway, Zutty left too not long after that. But Dicky left before, I took Dicky's place, see. And Zutty stayed around for a while, see, then Zutty left, see. Then we toured and then went from there to France, but not to work, we went there for a rehearsal. And most…

611.t: Not yet planning to stay: the car bought in Germany
611.s: Waters says he only wanted to see Paris and Europe, and recounts buying a car in Germany to ship to New York and the tax trouble that followed.
611.q: Yeah. I really didn't make my decision to stay, not like I did. I just wanted to see Paris and see a little bit of Europe, now my idea was to see Europe also.

611.t: The French and Italian tours with Coleman, then La Cigalle
611.s: Waters describes the French tour with Guy Lafitte reaching Casablanca, a six-week Italian tour, and leaving Coleman for the Cigalle with Jacques Butler.
611.ch: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
611.q: Anyway, I wasn't working no place, see, till we get some tours - I worked with the band, see, I worked with the band around Germany and -

611.t: Jacques Butler hires him at La Cigalle, 1955
611.s: Butler led the band at La Cigalle in Paris, where Waters arrived around 1955 still planning to go home.
611.ch: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
611.q: Well, in '55 or 6, I won't be exact all that, see. But around '55 or 6, somethin' like that -

611.t: Leaving the Cigalle for Belgium and Germany; Al Levrat's band
611.s: When Butler's band changed twice, Waters went to Belgium and to Germany; the third Cigalle band was led by Al Levrat, a Guadeloupean trombonist.
611.ch: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
611.q: Yeah, I went - ah, I stayed, that happened twice. Not - it happened twice that way. The one time that the band changed the names I went to Belgium and the guy, and Jacques Butler asked me to come back. The other time he changed the names I went to Germany, I think the first time I went to Germany.…

611.t: Touring Germany with local bands; the 1963 Koblenz festival
611.s: Waters played clubs with local bands and big tours with an English singer. He did not play the 1963 Koblenz expatriate festival but did a large festival with 15,000 people.
611.ch: Germany, Paris and return to America
611.q: Yeah, I bought it for that. It's a license, I forget what they call that license, it's a name for it, see, that you can carry it to the States without paying taxes.

611.s: Waters says he kept little contact with the States, but now sees Buddy Tate, Lockjaw, Sweets Edison and others constantly in Europe, earlier mostly Aaron Bridges and Peanuts Holland.
611.ch: Germany, Paris and return to America
611.q: Well, I didn't stay in touch. Well, that's, like I said before, that's a big fault of mine, my staying in touch with people. I mean that's something I've got to, even at my age now I've still got to learn. But I saw a few American musicians [ ] - not as many as now, which is the last few years, I…

611.t: Racism is international; Europe favouring bigger-name Americans
611.s: Waters says racism exists in Paris too and that European promoters often preferred big-name Black Americans like Sonny Stitt to him; he recalls leading an integrated California band in the 1940s.
611.q: Ah, that racism I've seen, I think that's international, you know? They have racism here in Paris, too, you'll see, particularly now, you know? And as far as the other thing is concerned, you have to come home back from Europe, but it's, you run through a little form of jealousy. [ ] this is…

611.t: Returning to La Cigalle and settling into Europe
611.s: A new offer from the Cigalle pulled him back to Paris instead of the States; he negotiated one day off a month for concerts, which helped establish his name.
611.ch: Germany, Paris and return to America
611.q: Oh, yeah, yeah, I kinda had it, mentally I felt that I was kinda gettin' up so people were dancing. Then when I went back the other time after that, I made an agreement with the guy to have a one day off a month, then I could do concerts. And then he stayed, I had a concert. 'Cause I'd write guys…

611.t: Forty years in Europe and making more money
611.s: He lived in Europe forty years, earned more there, and did solo work.

611.t: Being a living historian; Europe made up for the States
611.s: He says Europe's reception made up for what he did not earn in the States, and recalls playing organ concerts as a three-year-old boy wonder.
611.q: Yes well I’ve been in it a long time, see? I was playing as a soloist organ in the church and in concerts when I was three years old. I had my sister pumping the thing. I forget the name of that organ in that little church, the country organ. I couldn’t reach the pedals, you know, you play like…

611.t: Going out as a soloist in Germany, Switzerland and Belgium
611.s: Around 1960 Waters toured as a soloist, lived three and a half years in Hamburg and two in Mannheim, and bought his tax-free car there intending to go home.
611.ch: Germany, Paris and return to America
611.q: I stayed in Germany three years and a half in Hamburg, and two years in Mannheim [?]. And that was a period of the Cigalle too. And then I went back to the Cigalle again -

611.t: Audiences in Paris and Guadeloupean beguine music
611.s: Waters contrasts audiences now with then, recalls ten years at La Cigalle in Paris packed with Black soldiers, and describes beguine music played with a Guadeloupean trombonist.
611.q: See, they like the other music, they like their music. The Guadeloupe have their own thing, one of them, one of the music, one of the types of music that the Guadaloupians and the Martinique folks - they had a beguine, they call it, I think. A form of, I used to play it, I worked with one of those…

231.t: Stranded in Germany on a one-way ticket
231.s: A film producer sent him a one-way ticket to Germany with no contract signed; the American Consulate makes Lee Bouveau pay for lodging.
231.q: : I don't get to realize nothing. Take it the way it goes. The film company wanted to get a signature from the agent that told them about me and they paid the one-way ticket to be sure I would be there. Send me a round-trip ticket? No, that was too much to do. They send me a one-way ticket, it's…

231.t: Why he did not ask Bouveau for a ticket home
231.s: Nierenberg presses why he stayed four years; Bubbles says the Consulate had made him its responsibility and he waited on it.
231.q: Listen, I wanted to get a ticket back but I'm not asking him because the American Consulate took over the point which was most interesting to me. Whatever the American Consulate said, that's what

231.t: Staying to make a name in Europe so he could bring Buck over
231.s: He says he stayed to establish himself and earn enough to bring Buck to Europe.
231.q: Was to make a name sufficient enough and make enough money that I could get Buck to come over. That was

231.t: Why he went to Europe: low pay in the States and a ten-day job
231.s: He explains that salary cuts and no work at home made the $1,000-a-week offer attractive; he expected to be gone ten days while Buck was out of prison.
231.q: are you on the way where you got there? Where did you get there? How can I make money in there, there ain't no theater, best I'd get is maybe $150 or $200 for the week.

231.t: England in 1930: the Palladium with Gracie Fields
231.s: After Blackbirds Buck and Bubbles went to England, splitting top billing with Gracie Fields and playing the Cafe de Paris.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: He set it up but he messed it up after that, so we had to go on our own. So we went to England to the Palladium, splitting headlines with Gracie Fields, Gracie Fields was an English comedienne. And all the variety shows there. We played the Cafe de Paris. We played all the variety theaters there.

231.t: The finale, newspaper write-ups and Transatlantic Rhythm in London
231.s: He introduces the creators in the finale and was written up in every city; in 1936 he went to London for the short-lived Transatlantic Rhythm.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: I'm preaching this sermon to show It ain't necessa, ain't necessa, ain't necessa, ain't necessa, ain't necessarily so." Now the finale is "I'm on My Way," which Porgy sings. He comes back to find Bess, but Bess is gone with me and then we do the finale, 'cause I introduce everybody that does the…

231.t: A small revue while Buck was in jail, and the Germany offer
231.s: Working a little revue with Sonny Greer on 46th Street, he was seen by an agent who offered $1,000 a week to come to Germany for a film.
231.q: And something else I wanted to tell you about. Now, pick up on this one. Now, I'm in New York and Buck is in jail and while he's in jail I've got to worry about how I'm going to pay my bills. I ain't making no money. So I decided -- No, a guy saw me billed in a club, a little speakeasy like on 44th…

231.t: The cable from Lee Bouveau and AGVA's call for a bond
231.s: He got a letter and cable from an agent, learned he was a black man named Lee Bouveau, and AGVA advised a bond.
231.q: So what I did, I got a letter from England from a fellow who was in Germany concerning this review that I had and if I had

231.t: Landing in Frankfurt to find no contract, and the American Consulate
231.s: Arriving with seven dollars, Bubbles finds the producers had no contract signed, refuses to entertain soldiers for Bouveau, and gets the consulate to make Bouveau pay for his hotel.
231.q: So I got on the plane to go over there with about seven dollars in my pocket. Don't forget, all expenses paid. I could go a week without any money. They're going to take care of the hotel and everything. So what I got to worry about? That plane arrived in Frankfurt, Germany, the outskirts of…

231.t: Stranded in Frankfurt: a band leader's offer and an agent's $15 a show
231.s: At a cafe he knows the band leader but cannot take 20 marks a show; at the agent's office he is told Special Service pays $15 a show.
231.ch: Germany, Buck's death and ideas about life
231.q: So I go to the Bonnhoff -- that's the railroad station, you know -- Bonnhoff. I go to the Bonnhoff which is right across the street from the American Airlines office and that's when I spy that this band that's playing in this club next to that that was American and I knew the band leader.

231.t: Meeting Norman Thomas at the station and getting booked to Kaiserslautern
231.s: Band leader Norman Thomas gives him a card for 100 marks and the agent's office books him at $35 a show, sending him by train and crying with relief.
231.ch: Germany, Buck's death and ideas about life
231.q: ain't got no nothing. I got to do the best I can. So what I do I go to the Bonnhoff -- now I'm only across the street from the Bonnhoff, so I go across to the Bonnhoff and I'm just going in to watch the people coming and going. I don't know what told me to go, but I went. And who should be going to…

231.t: The Jolson show, a London court case and a job for her in Germany
231.s: He describes the non-variety show, winning a case in London, and taking her to Germany and teaching her to dance differently.
231.ch: Solo years, marriages and the Canadian party
231.q: No, the show had a cast of people doing a show called -- I forgot what that show consisted of -- it was not a variety show, no. "Members of Jolson" was the title of the show and we were all doing

231.t: Overseas with Bob Hope: the integration gag
231.s: Hope skipped their rehearsed dance, so Bubbles asked on stage if he believed in integration and told him to kiss him; three trips including Vietnam, he the only black performer.
231.ch: Television, the stroke and later reflections
231.q: was I asked Bob Hope if he believe in integra-tion. And his answer was to be yes. I say his answer was to be that. If he said no, I wouldn't be able to do the gag. So when he said yes, I did the gag on our first show that we did overseas following him not doing the dance that we had rehearsed…

231.s: American jokes like the window-shades gag did not land, so they changed the material and kept other bits.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: No, they're the same, but we had to change it around to make it meet with their sense of viewing. Because what was humorous to America wasn't humorous to English.

231.t: Entertaining the Duke and Duchess at Ascot
231.s: Corrected to 1936, he describes being driven in a Rolls Royce to entertain royalty at a fireside, finding it too nonchalant, and declining a party invitation.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: Yeah, this was the first time we was on television -- no this was the first broadcast television -- I think it was in 1936, not 1930. '30 we went on the radio -- we did a television broadcast in 1936. You understand? And it was their first broadcast of television, in '36. And we went out with…

231.t: A taped act reaches Wiesbaden; Lou Irwin gets him home for the Bill Robinson Story
231.s: A woman recorded his act and sent it to Special Service headquarters; Lou Irwin then got him a part in the Bill Robinson picture and Bob Hope soon asked for him.
231.ch: Germany, Buck's death and ideas about life
231.q: So I get back here, leaving

80.t: Gigging around New York; Red Richards takes him to Europe in 1968
80.s: After Philadelphia he did club dates at places like Eddie Condon's and Jimmy Ryan's; in 1968 Red Richards's Saints and Sinners took him to Europe for the first time, where people knew him from Fats.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: Gigged a bit, yeah, with this group, that group. Working down Eddie Condon's, here and there, and with different groups.

80.t: The jumping German club where young fans adored the band
80.s: On the Red Richards European tour a huge German club's young crowds, new to this music, kissed and danced with the band, and the manager signed them for a return.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: No, no. No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. We had a heck of a thing there, though. It's a big thing. It was jumping, and had two bands in there, and it's a big place, and they're doing -- yeah, yang, yang, yang-yang-yang, yang -- oh man! You know. God doggy!

80.t: Standing through sets with his cane and refusing a stool
80.s: He refused chairs to avoid being pitied, toughened up, and eventually forgot where he left his cane, and went to Europe twice with the band.
80.q: Yes it did. It did. And now, the fellows in the band, and a lot of the bosses, managers, would say Would you like to have a chair? Would you -- or a stool? I said no. No, thank you very much. Because I didn't want to -- back in my mind, I didn't want to say well, Herman, we have to let you go…

80.t: Capacity crowds and the twelve-day itinerary of the 1968 tour
80.s: Wilson reads the 1968 itinerary from Antwerp to Schaffhausen, twelve one-nighters in a row, with full houses wherever they played.
80.q: No, I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't -- no, no. But -- I may have had something to -- you know, because I mean -- well not to do with it, but I think it might have carried a little weight, since they said they were going to bring Herman Autrey. I'll put it that way.

80.t: Antwerp concert and keeping moving by plane, bus and taxi
80.s: They flew into Antwerp, ate at friends' homes, played a spacious hall, and then rose after a couple of hours' sleep to catch the next plane or bus.
80.q: Yeah, we got in -- yeah, because went down to friends and had dinner, had -- they knew some people there, and we went to their homes, and had dinner, fooled around with dinner. We came to the place to play, the concert, and there was -- as I remember -- it was quite spacious, quite a nice place,…

80.t: The dark Star Club in Hamburg after the rock bands
80.s: At the Hamburg Star Club the audience, used to rock, had never heard anything like the band; girls climbed on the stand and the manager offered a six-week contract.
80.q: No, they were -- when we got there they were in -- (laughs). They were playing, you know. And began, and as we went down the side trying to get figure how

80.t: European fans who knew every Fats Waller record; publicity
80.s: Fans compared how bands treated tunes they had on dozens of records, and the group got big posters and attention in each town.
80.q: No, {unintelligible} especially the kids, you know, people dancing, and everything, because it's so dark and you didn't know what the hell you -- you'd really have to know everybody in there to be bumping into somebody and saying hello Joe, what the hell. They didn't have no lights in there, and…

80.t: Flying into Spain over buttermilk skies
80.s: He describes the beauty of landing in Spain, the sea, whitecaps and the airfield beside the water.
80.q: Yeah, they had some television, they -- well in Spain, I don't know why it came to my mind. Well, the first time we'd been in Spain, and oh, it was so pretty. The flying in, the skies looked like buttermilk. I mean they said buttermilk skies, and that's -- maybe that's what they meant, because we…

80.t: Wheelchair dash to a TV studio, then by train through French vineyards
80.s: They rushed from the plane to a cold, damp studio for a TV show and a concert, then took a train through France to visit a doctor who made wine near Limoges.
80.q: Now, we hit the ground, okay, come on fellows, you've got to run like hell. I used to get me a wheelchair, had me a wheelchair standing by, you know, 'cause so that I couldn't move like the other guys, by the time you grab your coat here, and grab your luggage, and get this and do the other, and…

80.t: Paris traffic, bicycles and an underground club with no elevator
80.s: In Paris he marveled at the traffic and fearless cyclists and sat in at a club many flights underground, hard on his bad leg.
80.q: Let me see, we were there a couple of days. Was it two, or three days? But what happened, coming through the city there, man, whew! I never saw so much traffic.

80.t: Meeting American expatriates: Coleman, Nicholas, Mezzrow, Bishop, Waters
80.s: In Europe he saw Bill Coleman, Albert Nicholas, Mezz Mezzrow, Walter Bishop and Benny Waters, old friends who had settled abroad.
80.q: But I didn't meet him -- I didn't see him then, because last time I saw him -- his son, he must have been about 12 or 13. I saw him on 126th Street, here in New York, you know, because

80.t: Returning through Germany and London, and the collapse of the 1969 tour
80.s: After the 1968 trip they came back via London without playing there; the follow-up bookings in 1969 collapsed along with the promoter.
80.q: No. No, and that's -- I really -- I'm sorry about that, because when this man gave us this other booking, and they liked the band so much in Hamburg, and they had attached to-cut so much to our booking on the next one we did, were supposed to come back over, and we -- from London we were supposed…

80.t: Never played London; Stockholm and Montreux; finding the 'Sugar' album
80.s: He never played London but did play Stockholm and Montreux; Wilson reads off the details of the Sugar album, recorded in the Black Forest on April 1-2, 1968.
80.q: Oh yes. We left (unintelligible) 2nd we were going to Stockholm, and other thing, and I think I asked you, Switzerland there, and mentioned a friend of yours -- Simmen Johnny Simmons.

80.t: His first European trip in 1968, arranged through Hugues Panassie
80.s: After the Toronto record came out he first went to Europe in 1968; Hugues Panassie, whom he met in 1938, was the main reason, with fans waiting to see him.
80.q: Well, Red had, as you know, been to Europe, oh, my God, eight or ten times, about five or six times. Everybody had been over more than Herman had. And --

80.t: The six-week Hamburg contract lost to the booker's divorce
80.s: A lucrative return tour fell through when the man booking the European dates split with his wife and partner; Panassie advised but did not book.
80.q: him and wanted us to come back, because we were -- we weren't going to be in Germany, weren't going to be there much longer. We was getting ready to come back to the States.

91.t: Playing with Willie Lewis in Paris
91.s: He joined Willie Lewis's band at a late-hour club in Paris, met Reinhardt, Grappelli and Combelle, and recorded later.
91.q: Well, it was. I was tremendously impressed. I had heard so much about of Paris, and I started playing at this club, which was a late hour club; you know, you played until the last spending customer left, and that could be 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning, and maybe even later.

91.t: Arranging for the BBC, Scottish jazz players and living in Maida Vale
91.s: He arranged for Henry Hall's band, praised Scottish jazz players, and lived in Maida Vale near the studios.
91.q: Speaking of the restrictions about my playing, I was not allowed to play, you know, in personal appearances, but I could do recordings, which I did.

91.s: Permit limits forced him to leave the country periodically, which let him set up concerts on the Continent.
91.q: Well, I would only get a permit for a limited number of weeks or months and after which I would have to leave the country and then apply for a re-entry permit, which was always granted, fortunately -- but this gave me, you know, an excellent opportunity and reason to set up concerts on the…

91.t: Dating the move from Paris to London
91.s: Carter and Berger work out that he returned to Paris in July 1935 and reached London in March-April 1936.
91.q: Well, I guess I went back to Paris at that point, it seems to me, it must have been about July -- some time in July.

91.t: Continental tours and the international band in Holland
91.s: He toured France, Holland, Sweden and Denmark, taking an international band from London to Holland.
91.q: Well, I suppose sometimes I did. But usually it was, you know, I knew when I was going to have to leave, and I would set up a series of concerts.

91.t: Racial situation in Europe versus the United States
91.s: Carter found Europeans accepted him as a human being, though he knew what he was returning to.
91.ch: Returning to the US and the Savoy band
91.q: Oh yes -- quite definitely. I did. Yes. Of course, I had lived practically all of my life, prior to going to Europe, I had lived in New York, which was maybe a little better than some of the areas below, you know, south of the Mason/Dixon line.

91.t: Origins of the State Department Middle East tour
91.s: Berger conceived the tour; USIA accepted a proposal for 21 cities in 7 countries in December 1975 and January 1976.
91.q: Well, that came about because when I was doing a semester at which I was at Princeton, Dr. Berger, with whom I am talking here, said he would certainly like to see this happen. And I think it was almost like a dream of his, the way it followed through, and it was another one of those things that I…

91.t: European views of American jazz and white players
91.s: Europeans in 1935 were caught up in American music, and some still doubt white players as jazz originators.
91.ch: The Savoy band and the Swing era
91.q: Let me see ... what was I hearing? I guess I was ... like, I can't remember, no. No. I don't remember. I know that with the people like Charles Delauney, DeLome, you know, who did what I remember as being the first discography, maybe there was one before him; I don't know. And oh, Hugh Pannassie Le…

91.t: Touring and first visits to Japan
91.s: He first toured Japan in 1953-54 with Jazz at the Philharmonic and returned in 1973.
91.q: Then I returned in 1973, which was like 20 years later, and now I'm going again this coming April, '77.

91.s: Arriving in Copenhagen, Carter was greeted by a cheering crowd and carried to a hotel reception arranged by Kai Ewans.
91.q: Well, obviously, they did. They certainly knew me; they knew me much better than I had realized. I had what I might say was an interesting experience.

91.t: Impressions of the tour: audiences and Islam
91.s: Carter felt they missed ordinary people and seminar time, while Berger notes full houses and the musicians' interest in Islam.
91.q: And it was very, very well received. All along the way. We met some very, very interesting people; I felt a couple of things. I felt that we didn't get to play enough of the masses, you know what I mean? The common people, that we would like to have reached, and I think that our original idea was…

91.t: Leaving for London to arrange for Henry Hall and the BBC
91.s: Leonard Feather's letter brought him to London to arrange for the BBC dance orchestra under union limits on playing.
91.q: Well, I received a letter from Leonard Feather, and wanting to know if I would be interested in coming to London to arrange for the BBC dance orchestra,

91.t: Willie Lewis's cable and the decision to go to Europe
91.s: Domestic troubles and Willie Lewis's invitation led Carter to leave for Paris with his daughter, thinking of staying permanently.
91.q: Well, in all honesty, I wasn't sure, but I guess that when I made up my mind to go, I probably had the idea of staying forever because I took my young daughter with me, who had been in custody of my wife, and I was very, very angry about this, and I wanted her with me.

91.t: Deciding to go home and Willie Lewis's band
91.s: Carter wanted to see the Swing Era at home; Willie Lewis's Paris group later saw members go to Cairo.
91.q: Yes, and I thought I'd like to come back and see, you know, look the scene over and see if maybe I could do something, you know, with it, on it or in it. Or as part of it. And I also did think, though, at that time that I might be returning to Europe, to England at some time ...

75.t: Leaving Bryant for Europe with Bobby Martin
75.s: Ramirez and Glyn Paque left Willie's band for Bobby Martin's European offer in 1937; Ramirez missed the boat and followed later.
75.q: Oh yeah. Well, that's why we left the band, myself and Glyn Paque... We were (?)the last ones(?) in Willie's band to leave. We had Mike Ray, Bob McRae and... Bass Hill -- Bass Hill was in the band.

75.t: Paris World's Fair, the film L'Alibi and Bobby Martin's band
75.s: Martin's band played the Exposition pavilion and a cabaret scene in an Erich von Stroheim film, with personnel including the McRae family member Bob McRae.
75.q: Yeah. He came here for a while. So he came over to bring the musicians over to the World's Fair in Paris. So that was the thing. We were supposed to work in the Bronx(?), and... What the hell was the name of that place? Anyway, we played at the (?) Pavilion at the World's Fair. We also made a movie…

75.t: The "Sportsman Musician" and European racial attitudes
75.s: He skied and swam while others drank, and thought racial attitudes in France and Switzerland far better than in America.
75.q: Well, I wasn't pretty young in those days, you know. I was the youngest in the band, and they would say... They called me the Sportsman Musician. You know, while the

75.t: A weekend in London and the Exposition year
75.s: He visited London briefly to hear Ambrose's band, and they sort out whether the Paris Exposition was 1937 or later.
75.q: Yeah, in a sense. I wanted to see Ambrose's band. Really we went up over there, because they used to say... I mean, when they were in Paris they used to say their band didn't play like this... They were playing an engagement with Raymond Tour(?)... It was a good band.

75.s: After a layoff in Belgium where he fell sick, the band opened at the Mephisto in Holland, the Pshorr Dance Hall, Bern and Heck's.
75.q: off in Belgium. I remember it was like day and night. It was not like Switzerland at all. I got very sick and almost passed away.

75.t: Stranded as war nears: Paris, Jimmy Monroe, the night train
75.s: With Bobby gone, Ramirez found Americans were being repatriated via Paris, met Jimmy Monroe, and escaped by night train through Belgium to Rotterdam.
75.q: : Bass said...I don't know how... Bass decided to go one way or the other; I don't remember just how. He went...I don't know, he went somewhere, and I was left alone. So how I heard... The consul told me that there was an organization that was taking Americans back home, but you had to go to Paris.…

75.t: Waiting in Rotterdam; the Three Dukes and Willie Lewis
75.s: While waiting for a Saturday boat, Ramirez sat in at Den Haag with the Three Dukes and met Wilson Myers.
75.q: Well, it was.... I don't know. It was about a week. Something like that. Our boat was leaving on a Saturday night at about 11 o'clock.

75.t: Eindhoven band and the Gestapo search on the train to Denmark
75.s: He led a band in Eindhoven, then on the way to meet Bobby in Denmark, Gestapo on the train seized Glyn Paque's dice and record player.
75.q: : Speaking about Harlem, in ...(?)... When Bobby left... You see, Linkback(?) and I got together somehow or other. We played up in Helleman(?), Einholden.... Oh, we were supposed to meet Bobby in 1938 at the National Scala in Denmark. Last time, you know, the doctor was here from Holland, they…

75.s: They played the National Scala for dancing, an American novelty act, around New Year 1939 alongside Kai Ewans's big band.
75.q: : Yeah. Attraction(?) (?)s, and jazz, old jazz. At that time, you see...American bands in those days... It was a novelty. They'd say, "American musicians from the Cotton Club and all that." You had (?)Wayne Wright(?), Little Lips... [LAUGHS]

75.s: Bobby and Johnny Russell left early; Ramirez and Glyn Paque, Bass Hill remained, played Bern, then left as war fears rose.
75.q: : Oh, well before. Yeah, he just left us there. From there, we went to Dancing Chiquita(?) in Bern. And from Bern, that's when we left.

75.t: Home looked strange after the Nordic countries
75.s: Returning to Harlem felt dreary and unreal after Europe, and he praises Denmark.
75.q: strange, very strange. Having been with Nordics a good deal of the time, you know, ha! -- Harlem looked very dreary. My own relatives and my own close friends looked very unreal, you know. There's something about the life in Europe that's just a little bit different than America.

75.s: On the 1968 tour he found Hammond organs scarce and was given pump organs.
75.ch: Eddie Heywood, the organ and later work
75.q: It was all right. The only difficulty we had was you couldn't find a Hammond organ everywhere at that time. I went to Europe, and it was very...you know, it was scarce as far as organs were concerned.

75.t: Itinerary: Chez France, Zurich and Basel
75.s: After about three years in Europe, the band played Chez France, then the Singapore in Zurich and the Odeon in Basel as war loomed.
75.q: Let's see, '37, '38, '39... I arrived here on New Year's Day or Christmas, around Christmas or New Year's, 1940. Just three years.

75.t: Martin Roman, Freddy Johnson, Hawkins and Princess Beatrix's birth
75.s: He recalls Martin Roman and Freddy Johnson in a concentration camp, Coleman Hawkins in Holland in 1938, and hearing "A Foggy Day" the day Beatrix was born.
75.q: : I met a piano player named Martin Roman. He was from Germany. He was Jewish. He was the piano player with a band called Adde(?) Roselander(?). He would support Louis Armstrong.... A bunch of good musicians... I never saw him again. But Martin Roman spent time in a concentration camp with Freddy…

382.t: Recording with British musicians; singing in London
382.s: She enjoyed the British musicians; Hue magazine's photo essay on her singing in London in 1954.
382.q: They were good. We had a good time. When I went over in '48 -- well, this is '54. In '54, I went over there -- I went into a club. I went into a club on Bond Street. I forget the name of the club.

382.t: Touring the British Isles in 1948: Cardiff and the Royal Theater
382.s: She toured to Wales, played Cardiff and the Royal Theater, and had a great reception.
382.q: Yeah. I played in Cardiff. I played in Cardiff and -- Oh you talk about a tour! I left London and I got to Dublin, Ireland on St. Patrick's Day and I played --

382.t: Length of her stays and the north: Ireland, Dundee
382.s: She stayed about sixty days in one place, enjoyed Dublin, a steak, and Scotland's hospitality.
382.q: Yeah. I was longer than that in '53. I stayed quite a bit both times I was over there. I didn't come right back. I stayed as long as I could, you know, on my work thing

382.t: Touring with the World's Greatest Jazz Band and the Dutch connection
382.s: Ted Easton heard her at the concert, which led to the Holland album; she tours with the band.
382.q: Yeah. Well, I was on tour with The World's Greatest Jazz Band in that year. And we played Amsterdam, and Ted Easton showed up and asked me to this album for him.

382.t: The Atlantic Club and Swedish club life
382.s: She describes the club, its membership, its owner Bo, and the contrast with younger clubs.
382.q: It was at the time. When we played the first engagement there -- you know, when we had the three days -- Bo Stemhammer, who owned the club and operated the club, they had just moved in there. And they were still in the process of decorating the club.

382.t: How American musicians tour Europe and local rhythm sections
382.s: Musicians go club to club and are treated well; local players are good, though audiences vary.
382.q: It's very good, you know, it's very good because like I said it was not easy to take a band over, but individual musicians can go over there and appear all over the Continent and the British Isles and one of the advantages there, one of the arrangements that is very good on tour like that as…

382.t: Copenhagen, a Swedish television show and her 65th birthday
382.s: Only one night in Copenhagen, a lukewarm response, and a televised show in Stockholm where she celebrated her 65th birthday.
382.q: Oh, yeh, yeh, well, we didn't -- we only did one night in Copenhagen, and that would be the first tour, we didn't go back there again. But on that first tour, we got around quite a bit. We played several towns in Germany and in Holland and a lot of times we didn't make the second time we were out,…

382.t: Travelling abroad with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
382.s: She went to Europe nearly every year with the band; her earlier trips were Britain in 1948 and 1953-54.
382.q: Yeah, well that's been a long time, man. That's been a long, long time. These were taken in Stockholm.

382.t: Her two trips to Britain and Ireland
382.s: She played the London Casino in 1948 and a variety circuit in 1953-54, transposing arrangements for pit bands.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: Yeah, the first time I went over was in 1948, but I was still doing - oh, 'Loch Loman' got me there. I was supposed to go there in 1938 and then the war broke out and there was no exchange of artists between the two Continents and so I really didn't get there until 1948. But 'Loch Loman', when I…

382.t: Black Broadway at Newport and Adelaide Hall
382.s: An aside about the 1979 production Black Broadway and Adelaide Hall's recordings in England.
382.q: Well I haven't gotten to London yet, but when I finally got there, I lived with Adelaide while I was there.

382.t: Nice Jazz Festival tribute to Louis Armstrong
382.s: She appeared at Newport and Nice with the band; the unveiling of Louis's bust in Nice.
382.q: Yeah. I had appeared on two previous Newport Jazz Festival programs. One in Providence quite before the Newport Jazz Festival moved to New York. And, of course, I was on a bill that the first Newport Jazz Festival in New York on that section in which Benny Carter appeared, and Teddy Wilson…

382.s: In 1948 she went to the UK; the English resented the swing Loch Lomond more than the Scots.
382.q: Yeah. In '48 when I went over, you know I was afforded this trip to "Loch Lomond"--the British Overseas Air Corporation sponsored my trip from London to Scotland. And I sang "Loch Lomond" on the shores of "Loch Lomond", wondering what the reaction was going to be. Because previously -- but the…

382.s: Chittison left the U.S. in the late 1920s and travelled in Europe and India, working for Jacoby; he settled in Ohio.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: But Herman Chittison was one of the musicians that left the United States very early in the era. I would say he probably left the United States

71.t: Deciding to go to Europe in 1949
71.s: After years of hearing about Paris, he saved money to go with drummer Wallace Bishop and trumpeter Merle Stepter.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: Well another case like in California. I wanted to come to New York from California, I'd heard so much about it. So now, I'd heard so much about it, England and France and people would come back when I was in the Teresa, like Joe Louis would go there on exhibition boxing tours, he'd say 'Buck, you…

71.s: After Panassie hired a French rhythm section, he stayed nine months, learned about postwar Parisian life and picked up slang.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: Yes. I still might have a sea stomache, I don't know. But I know that boat used to rock and all I'd just roll with it, I hever would get, I never got dizzy. The only time you get dizzy is drinking that red wine that they keep putting in front of you for dinner. You drink red wine with the dinner,…

71.t: Sightseeing in Europe: Joan of Arc, Carcassonne, Stonehenge
71.s: He enthuses over historic sites such as Joan of Arc's, Carcassonne and Stonehenge.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: like going to Newark, New Jersey. Because everybody has been there and actually some of them have been there too many times. Another thing I liked, I never could get over these old places like that we had read about. For instance, where they burned Joan of Arc, that's still beautiful. They've got…

71.t: Switzerland, the Blue Note in Paris, and returning home
71.s: He played with Bill Coleman in Bern, did Paris Blue Note with Lil Armstrong and Don Byas, then went home while Bishop stayed.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: Switzerland has got the Alps and I used to go play in the Chikita Club in Bern, especially in the winter. And you could just see thousands of people going on up the mountains and everybody's got skis.

71.s: In 1953 he returned for Mezzrow with Big Chief Moore, Taps Miller and Lindy Hop dancers, bringing his wife.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: And dancing. And we had two teams from the Savoy Ballroom that was doing the Lindy Hop. So that was a nice trip too. That was a very nice, and I took my wife on that one. I took my wife. It was nice.

71.t: Touring France and Morocco with Mezzrow
71.s: Mezzrow ordered regional food for the band, and Yannick Bruynoghe was road manager on tours of France and Morocco.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: When I was with Mezzrow we played all over France and all over the small countries and I was happy that Mezzrow was there because he knew the exact favorite food of whatever district we were in, you know. Like one district over there is, their specialty is coq au vin. The cock with the....

71.t: Invited to England: tours with Buddy Tate, Dickie Wells and others
71.s: Jack Higgins invited him to England, where he first brought his own band, and returned in 1961 with Sir Charles and Jimmy Witherspoon.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: Yes, it sure is. Then while I was in Belgium I got a call from Jack Higgins. (LAUGHTER). To ask if I would like to come to England and play with Humphrey Lyttleton. Yes, that was one of the main things I wanted to do because I had heard a lot about Humphrey. Even Louis used to tell me about…

71.t: More dates with Lyttelton and Alex Welsh
71.s: He returned a few times to play with Lyttelton and recalls meeting Alex Welsh at Essen.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: Then I went back, I went back and I didn't play too many more dates with Humphrey because I had come home from that special trip. But then I went back to or three other times and played with Humphrey. Which was a gas, you know.

71.s: Clayton and Dance discuss why European fans are more appreciative, including Ellington's rare visits.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: Oh yes. All the difference in the world. You know there is, there is fans here that are just as great to you I think. Now you take the Duke Ellington fan club, you know that club, they're all dedicated fans, especially of Duke's. But it seems to me that all the people over there are that way, not…

71.t: Denmark with John Darville and tenor Jesper Thilo
71.s: He toured Denmark, played the Montmartre, and praises tenor Jesper Thilo.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: Yes, well he's French but he's livin' over there, so. I made a very nice recording called "Swinging the Blues" with all of these fellows. Then I went to Denmark and I played with John Darville there.

71.t: Playing with Humphrey Lyttelton and touring with Big Joe Turner
71.s: He enjoyed playing with Lyttelton, made two albums with him, and toured with Joe Turner, trying Newcastle brown ale.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: They still talk about that in Geneva. They say do you remember that time? I say, yes I remember I always will. But after that I went to, had the pleasure of playing with Humphrey and his band. That was nice. Two or three times maybe four.

71.t: Panassie's invitation and Bishop's tearful boarding
71.s: Panassie had invited them, and Clayton, who learned French in New York, sailed with Bishop weeping over his wife.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: having trouble with his wife. She was putting him down. So we all saved up enough money and caught the Isle de France and went over there. But before we went Paradisio has been to New York, he came to New York somewhere down in that time.

71.s: Based in Paris he guested with Bill Coleman in Switzerland, earning hundreds of dollars a night.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: to Switzerland to play with Bill Coleman's band as guest artist. You see when I wasn't playing with my band I played all over Switzerland and made a lot of money. Sometimes they paid me three or four hundred dollars for one night. And I didn't believe them. Me and Bishop would say, gee, they must…

77.t: Being put on a pedestal in Europe
77.s: Celebrities were treated with deference in Europe and returned to America with a bigger name and contracts.
77.q: I want to tell you, Chris -- excuse me for cutting you off, but the thing of it was, when you were a celebrity, when you went to Europe, even the most prejudiced parts, you were put on a pedestal. The people in Europe would put you on a pedestal whereby even from you leave America, you'd have to go…

77.t: Length of the Show Boat run, Edith Day's jealousy, the King and Queen
77.s: The show ran about eleven and a half months; star Edith Day was jealous of Robeson's notices; Robeson went off pitch when told the King and Queen were attending.
77.q: 'Showboat' ran about 11 1/2 months. Now, I tell you, there was a little jealousy there in 'Showboat'. Edith Day, who was our star -- when the --

77.t: Introducing Noel Coward songs at the Dorchester; Jack Jackson record
77.s: Coward heard her at the Dorchester and had her introduce "Two Cigarettes in the Dark", "Miss Otis Regrets" and "I Travel Alone"; a British fan has just sent her old records.
77.q: Well, Vic sings it all the time. How did that come about? Well, Mr. Coward used to frequent the Dorchester all the time, you know, and the King -- he was the

77.t: Touring the English provinces after Show Boat
77.s: After Show Boat she toured provincial theaters in England, Scotland and Ireland, was the first Black woman at the Argyle, and introduced "Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day".
77.q: I went back to -- oh, no. When Showboat closed, I toured all -- toured the theaters in th e provinces of England. The Argyle Theater -- oh, I hope I can find that record -- I mean that article, just a beautiful article. I think I was the first colored girl ever worked there.

77.t: Casino de Paris after Josephine Baker; Cecile Sorel and Gustav Wally
77.s: The Casino de Paris owner hired her after hearing her at Le Grand Ecart, where Jean Patou dressed her; in Vive Paris she worked with Cecile Sorel and the Swedish prince Gustav Wally.
77.q: That's right, Casino de Paris. Well, I tell you what, when Josephine Baker went to the Folies-Bergere, that's when Mr. Barner, who had the Casino de Paris, had me come down, and I don't think I did an audition for -- for the Casino de Paris. I didn't do an audition for Casino de Paris because he…

77.t: Copenhagen contract through Mrs. Bach and the National Scala
77.s: On the prince's word the artistic director sent her a six-month contract for the National Scala, and she returned twice a year with standing contracts.
77.q: So I said, oh, I'd love to go. And I said -- he said, I tell you what. If you ever want to go to Denmark, you write -- write Bach -- her name was Bach, Mrs. Bach. Her first name will come to me. She was the artistic director of this -- of the National Scholar in Copenhagen. He said, if you ever…

77.t: Going back and forth, and the color film Radio Parade of 1935
77.s: She spent years in Europe with visits home; in 1935 she sang "Dark Shadows" with a choir in Radio Parade of 1935, a first color process film in England.
77.q: But now, listen here, now, '35, if you remember now -- when did I go to the Palladium, because I remember in 1935, that's when I made that picture.

77.t: Whether the English film was shown in America; Isadora Duncan
77.s: She thinks the film was seen in the US; she never met Isadora Duncan.
77.q: I think it did, because I think somebody told me. If I'm not mistaken, I think somebody told me they saw that film. But I didn't see it. But I understand that it was very good, very good.

77.t: Grand Terrace with Earl Hines and going to Europe in 1929
77.s: After returning from Europe in 1929 she worked a few weeks with Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace, did Show Boat in London with Paul Robeson, and kept going back and forth.
77.q: Yeah, it was pretty fancy. But the Sunset was -- now listen, I tell you one thing, in 1929 -- in 1929 I know I went to work at the with Earl Hines. At the Grand Terrace. I'm sure.

77.t: Homesickness in Europe and "The White Cliffs of Dover"
77.s: She was not truly homesick but wanted to return to Chicago after recording; the song made her cry at Fred Payne's club in Paris, and she went home.
77.ch: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
77.q: Well, I don't say that I was homesick, but there were times when I would want to go back. Now, for instance, every time I would leave Chicago and come to New York to record, I couldn't get back to Chicago fast enough. I always left on the next train.

77.t: Mabel Mercer, Jimmy Daniels and Bricktop's Paris club
77.s: She recalls Mabel Mercer in the Show Boat choir, her circle of friends, and nights at Bricktop's club in Paris with Louis Coles and Jimmy Donahue.
77.q: 1935. That was it, Radio Parade of 1935. And the Casino de Paris, as I say, was Vive Paris with Cecile Sorel. Don't forget her because she was a marvelous woman, the actress of France, you know. And incidentally, talking about Showboat, don't forget now, Mabel Mercer was in the choir, in the big…

77.t: From Monte Carlo to a benefit in London and Leslie Hutchinson
77.s: Noble Sissle's telegram let her into England for a flood benefit, where she sang with Leslie Hutchinson at the piano before Alfred Butt, Hammerstein and Kern.
77.q: Well, I tell you, I went from -- I went from New York to Monte Carlo just on a visit, took a friend of mine, a girlfriend of mine, Bert Williams' oldest niece, Lottie Tyler. So we went to Monte Carlo just -- a little fun. And while I was there --

77.t: Auditioning at Drury Lane for Queenie against Maizie Ailing
77.s: She sang after Ailing for the Queenie part in Show Boat with Paul Robeson and was picked because they wanted the real thing.
77.q: white woman named Maizie Ailing who was absolutely marvelous. She was the last word. She was a big woman, just what they wanted in Aunt Jemimy, and had the voice and -- she just had everything that you want. And she -- she sang, and then I sang.

67.t: Sam Wooding in Europe and the Barcelona recording
67.s: He joined Sam Wooding's band in 1928, toured Europe, and recorded in Barcelona and Paris, including one arrangement.
67.q: Sam Wooding was a band in New York and he turned down the Cotton Club, to rather go to Europe with his band than to play in the Cotton Club. That’s how Duke got in there. It wasn’t but Sam Wooding. So Sam took the band to Europe in 1927, the latter part of ‘27. And I joined Sam Wooding and went to…

67.t: Wooding's show band and the first night in Berlin
67.s: Wooding's band was an entertaining show band with singers, a comedian, Edith Wilson and chorus girls; opening in Berlin, waiters brought the band food in the dressing room.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: Sam I thought had one of the greatest bands I'd ever heard. It was a very good band. We did mostly -- it was an entertaining band.

67.t: Lead trumpet with Wooding and giving up jazz
67.s: He joined as lead trumpet because Bobby Martin could not do both jobs, stopped playing jazz for three years, and was caught up in the excitement of Europe.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: Oh, very -- oh yes. Yes. I thought that was the greatest thing in the world, the band. I jumped in that band and I was playing lead trumpet. That's the thing that [were] very important, money. I joined Sam Wooding as a lead trumpet player because Bobby Martin was the lead trumpet player and also…

67.t: Touring Germany, Spain, Vienna and Constantinople
67.s: Berlin was headquarters for long engagements across Germany, Spain, Vienna and Constantinople, with recordings made in Barcelona.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: So we -- we went with the show, we went all over Germany, played Hamburg, and most of our engagements were sometimes a month --

67.t: Leaving Wooding after hearing the Cotton Pickers
67.s: Feeling stale, Cheatham left in Paris, having fallen in love with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers records; Wooding himself felt unaffected by distance from America.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: Well, I came back to the states because I was -- listening a lot of times to this thing -- some recordings, especially Cotton-picker's Band. I fell in love with that band when I was in Europe. I heard them -- some of their recordings and I felt as though I need improvement -- I says, I'm getting…

67.t: Learning technique from an Argentine tango trumpeter in Biarritz
67.s: At the Biarritz casino he went daily to a trumpeter with the Canaro tango band to pick up techniques.
67.ch: Philadelphia, New York and Sam Wooding in Europe
67.q: Yes, oh yes. I had a few instructions from trumpet players in Europe, at that time. That I heard were doing things that I wanted to know how, they were doing them. One fellow from Argentina by name of [Canaro,] he was over there with the famous Tango Band, called the [Canaro] Brothers. They had at…

67.t: Cab Calloway's 1934 tour of Britain and Paris
67.s: The band played the London Palladium, Scotland, Manchester and a Paris concert; a jealous pit band blasted distortions, and the band tore the theater up.
67.q: And we also played -- we played a couple of theaters there, we did another theater, I think it was a benefit in London, I don't remember the name of the theater. We -- the pit band at this theater, they give us a hard time before we went on, because they announced Cab's band as a benefit. The pit…

67.t: Leaving Cab in 1939: Dandridge side date, then Europe as war begins
67.s: Albertson recalls his 1936 side date with Putney Dandridge, Teddy Wilson and Big Sid Catlett. He left Cab in 1939 to live in Europe, the war began as his ship blacked out, and he stayed in Paris playing for the Hot Club of France and recording for Swing, and later with Eartha Kitt in 1950.
67.q: Yes. I went to Europe. I went to Europe, with -- I wanted to live in Europe, I just said, I want to go back. Decided to go back, I wanted to live in Europe for awhile.

67.t: Realizing in 1967 that jazz would be taken seriously
67.s: Only in 1967, when calls and invitations to Europe began, did Cheatham see his importance; he also recalls his one record for Charles Delaunay.
67.q: I never had that feeling. I was just trying to push myself to learn so much and then, after 1967, I was beginning to get calls from people, asking questions, writing books and invited here to play this jazz thing, go to Europe. I went to Europe, I guess it was George Wein and (unintelligible). I…

67.t: Substituting for Buck Clayton in Nancy, France in 1950
67.s: In Europe in 1950 he took Buck Clayton's place at a packed concert where the audience first thought he was Buck and the musicians were nervous, then cheered.
67.ch: Latin bands, Wilbur DeParis and Goodman
67.q: Yes. Well, I went to Europe, at that time, mostly to get away, I was having a little matrimonial problem. And I just went to that, I took my horn, said I'm going to stay over there. Something stopped, me the war, no it wasn't the war, I didn't seem -- after I got there, I didn't seem to like it,…

67.s: The band was a sensation in Africa; Cheatham heard cow-horn, drum and marimba bands in Uganda and played on a Nairobi radio show, then toured Europe in 1960.
67.ch: Latin bands, Wilbur DeParis and Goodman
67.q: Oh yes, they entertained us most every country. We heard the best of their groups. We heard the bands played -- where they played cow horns on -- the entire band played horns, horns from the cow.

67.t: The Top Brass tour of Europe in 1967
67.s: A 15-day tour with Benny Morton, Clark Terry, Bobby Brookmeyer and Maynard Ferguson's big band, where he and Morton sat in with Maynard unpaid.
67.ch: Latin bands, Wilbur DeParis and Goodman
67.q: We had Nat Pierce, drummer, I never remember his name. The had a trio that Benny Morton and myself played -- the same trio played with Clark Terry and Bobby Brookmeyer. And then Maynard Ferguson's big band was on the program. And Benny Morton and myself sat in with Maynard's big band. Just for…

28.t: Germany in 1933: Hitler, marks and no race problem
28.s: Butler says he did not follow politics, just got paid in marks, and met no racial problem in Germany; he joined Charlie Turner's band.
28.ch: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
