28.q: Well, see, I didn't know that much about politics to really note. (Inaudible). All I know, that money was flowing and I was getting them marks and I was doing good.

28.t: Sailing to Europe in 1936 and starting at the Chez Florence
28.s: Butler crossed on the Ile de France in a Teddy Bear coat and joined Willy Lewis at the small Chez Florence in Paris, bringing new Roberta music and the covered tone learned from Henry Walton.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: Yeah. (Inaudible), I caught it right there. I said, well, Jack, now you've got to go in and play that thing with the covered tone. And I hit it right off.

28.t: The Willy Lewis seasonal circuit and picking up languages
28.s: The band wintered in France, spent spring in Egypt and summer at Knokke, Belgium, and Butler used Creole with West Indians to pick up French.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: I went to school and was studying, started studying right away. Now, here in wintertime we would stay there in France. Now, when you come into spring, we'd go to Egypt. And the summertime, we'd go to Knokke, Belgium. And in the fall we'd go to -- we'd go in between Knokke (PHONETIC) and we might go…

28.t: Alexandria: the Greek owner Pastudes, hotel pounds and Stardust
28.s: In Alexandria the owner Pastudes treated the band lavishly; Butler took a cheaper room and won over a cold audience with a Stardust solo.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: Beautiful. They had a man, his name was Pastudes (PHONETIC). This man was the feigningest man I'd ever seen, but this man was a handsome man, a Greek, Pastudes. Pastudes could smile and look like an angel, and he was a dark-complected man. And get mad and look like a devil looking at you, really.

28.t: Playing at King Farouk's wedding and leaving for Holland
28.s: Before summer the band left Egypt for Holland, having played King Farouk's wedding, and Chittison nearly got jailed again; Wilson Miles was passing himself off as a local.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: So we stayed there, but we had to leave. It was -- summertime was coming on, we had to go to Holland so Burns and Pastotis were looking at each other and Pastotis was getting eviler every day, so Burns wanted to stay there, but he says, I'll come back. We take off and get our business straight and…

28.t: Back at the Chez Florence among five kings; Paris as entertainment capital
28.s: Returning in spring, the band played for kings and royalty at the Chez Florence; Butler describes Paris as the hub of entertainment with Eddie South and Benny Peyton passing through.
28.ch: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
28.q: So we finished our contract and then we -- now this is springtime, we goes back into Chez Flordes, the place is called Chez Flordes. This is our place, that's where we were located there in Paris. It was the kings and all royalty. King George, Prince of Wales. I went down there, there were four…

28.t: Denmark concert with Svend Asmussen, Valaida Snow and Freddie Crump
28.s: Just before the Germans took Denmark he played a concert at Karpehollen with Svend Asmussen, Leo Mathisen, Roland Smith, Louis Sims, and mentions Valaida Snow and drummer Freddie Crump.
28.q: Now, there was a man, fellow named Sven Asmussen, come from Denmark. He looked like Stuff Smith, and he played just like Stuff Smith. He was a Dane, the swingingest rascal you ever heard. On the violin.

28.t: Racial strain on Black musicians and relief in Europe
28.s: Asked about Lester Young, Butler says Black musicians are under constant mental strain from racial headlines, which lifts abroad; some use the freedom to learn and others do not.
28.ch: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
28.q: Yes, indeed, I heard Lester Young. Yes, sir.Unfortunately, Lester didn't go to France -- or didn't stay a long time. It would have prolonged his life. I'll tell you why. You see, you can say what you want to, but a musician, he's under strain all the time.

28.t: Spending money in Holland and rumors of Hitler
28.s: The band arrived in Holland in fezzes with Egyptian spoils, was jailed for spending too fast, played a Dutch engagement and heard rumors about Hitler at the end of 1936 and in 1937.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: (Den Haag?) Dieve, Holland, now we comes into Holland with them fezes on. Fezes on and Willy Lewis had a diamond about seven carats and gold, and that was it, and the bags, and Egyptian -- Egypt is known for their beautiful leather work. We had bags, beautiful and in Egypt your tailors are East…

28.t: Benny Peyton's drumming and playing for European audiences
28.s: Drummer-bandleader Benny Peyton, long in Europe, knew how to make audiences understand jazz and was always working, and in Switzerland they wanted spirituals and St. Louis Blues.
28.ch: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
28.q: Benny Payton played the drums. He had a band. He always stayed around in Germany, mostly Austria -- Benny Payton, I think he was from Chicago. Then you had --

28.t: Back to Europe, leaving Willy Lewis for Ricco's Creole Band in Norway
28.s: When war broke out he left after being insulted by Burns at rehearsal, joined a Cuban band, Ricco's Creole Band, and toured Norway, where he started a small jazz club.
28.q: So, all right, after I had taken care of all of my business I went back. But now, this is in the summertime, I went back. And when I got back, the war was in -- so, I said, well, I'll go to Sweden, I can make my way around Europe now.

28.t: Belgian business venture with a millionaire after de Gaulle expelled the Americans
28.s: A Belgian millionaire invited Butler to open clubs after de Gaulle's order forced American forces out; the venture failed and the Paris owner complained he was not resting.
28.ch: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
28.q: Now, then I've got an idea to have business. See, this man coming in there with pheasants and all on his back, and counting money and everything, and when he first come in to sell it." there he was as poor as he could get. "Now we're going" In the meantime I met a man called Jean Paul Lauget…

117.t: Success in Europe at age 71 and doubts about the United States
117.s: Based in London for three and a half years and booked across the Continent, Freeman says a genuine jazz soloist is valued more as he ages.
117.ch: Harlem, race and life in Europe
117.q: I have been so lucky really, in and all the good white players who were later to become famous soloists, were very lucky that they had this music to use because without it, it might have gone into the studios where they would have become old and not wanted. There's a beautiful thing -- I do not…

117.t: Dexter Gordon's return to the States and being yourself
117.s: Dance and Freeman discuss Dexter Gordon's success after years abroad and whether Freeman would do as well at home.
117.ch: Harlem, race and life in Europe
117.q: Well, I heard Dexter Gordon one night at a concert, we were on the same show in -- it was in Verona, Italy, of course, and he --

117.s: Freeman says European pianists imitate Stacy and discusses his agent bringing American stars over and whether Stacy would tour.
117.ch: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
117.q: Well, the marvelous thing, if Jess could get to know, and this eventually he will, I suppose, hear this and read it, he's -- all the pianist I have

117.t: Gerald Lascelles's Beaulieu festival and first solo trips to Britain
117.s: Invited to a British festival, Freeman played with Chris Barber, then arranged solo tours with the Alex Welch band, coming two or three times yearly.
117.q: Then I started to go to Europe. I got -- let's see, George Wein gave a party -- George Wein had now moved into New York and in his apartment he gave a party for Gerald Lascelles, the Queen's cousin, and he invited me to the party and I met Gerald Lascelles, and he was all over me, we were very good…

117.t: Newport tours, Mexico and the West Berlin Philharmonic Hall
117.s: Freeman recalls tours with George Wein's all-stars, including opening West Berlin's Philharmonie, and a Copenhagen Tivoli festival, showing Europe's jazz market.
117.q: Well, of course, I wasn't staying there. I'd go back to the States after -- the tours were only for a couple of weeks, you see, and then I'd be back in the States.

117.t: Deciding to stay in Europe: the Breda festival and bookings
117.s: Freeman planned six months in Europe, was offered big money for one hour at the Breda festival, and is now booked about two years ahead.
117.q: It's too bad because I think it's a lovely country, but it's a damp, damp country. But then you see, I am sitting on top of all the work here, as I told you, it takes me such little time to get to places I have to play. I never know with whom or with what I am going to play, but I work as a soloist…

117.t: The pattern of European work: short sets, quick flights
117.s: Freeman describes 20 to 45 minute sets with local rhythm sections, German jazz clubs, and an eleven-minute closing spot at Hanover.
117.q: minutes sets a night, and not so long ago I went over to Hanover to do the impressario called and said, would you want to come over and close a show. A big jazz concert with a lot of wellknown people in Europe and I went over and there was 11 minutes left for me. They paid me before I went on, I…

117.t: American musicians meeting in Europe; Billy Butterfield's tour
117.s: Dance and Freeman discuss Europe as a market of many countries where American friends he hasn't seen in 20 years now visit.
117.q: Well, do you want to know an interesting thing, Helen. I see American jazz musician friends more in Europe than ever I saw them in the States because many of them were living in Florida, many in California, you know, spread all over the country, but I see them all, men I haven't seen

117.t: Records abroad and his European following
117.s: Freeman says anyone who made many records does well in Europe because audiences know them.
117.q: Yes, that's true, anybody who made a lot of records can do very well over here, because people remember the records. In fact, in concerts I do today, they'll come back and say you didn't play it that way on the record. They know, you see.

117.t: Declining a College Swing Band tour, then staying in Europe
117.s: Haggart persuaded him to decline a tour offer, but at Rotterdam a Dutch promoter offered Festival money and Robert Masters began handling him as a soloist.
117.ch: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
117.q: And so I took the letter, it was an offer to do a tour with the College Swing Band, incidentally, I go out with them very soon and do a tour of Germany in October.

117.s: Freeman says Britons have backed American dance music and jazz for seventy years and turn out seriously for American soloists.
117.q: Yes, I have a lot of -- well, I know everybody in London, and I know so many people throughout the U.K. and I played -- I must have played in the 16 years I have been coming here on and off, I must have played 100 cities, you know, and they are all jazz -- you know, you must

117.t: Playing with different groups across Europe; Red Norvo
117.s: Freeman plays with whoever is booked, avoids leading a group, and flies between concerts; Dance notes Red Norvo does the same.
117.ch: Harlem, race and life in Europe
117.q: But I want to say that I never know with whom or with what I am going to play so I play with all kinds of different styles, you know.

566.s: Starting on fans, Humes says European audiences are completely in your corner. In Sweden everything was paid for, and a driver and chauffeur looked after her.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: Well, when people over there like you they are really in your corner a hundred percent. And I've got so many fans and friends and things that I still hear from.

566.s: Bo Stenhammer booked her for a Swedish festival with a good band behind her. It was her only Swedish trip, in 1980, soon after her illness, and the organisers bent over backwards.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: Yes and a good one. I went over there for a festival and he had Bo Stenhammer. Has it every year. They wanted me to come back this year but with me being sick, I didn't. But I still ...

566.t: Swedish concerts, TV show and working with local musicians
566.s: She did a TV show and two club concerts, closing the show as the only American star. She brings no band or scores, only lead sheets, and the European musicians are excellent.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: I did a TV show. And then I just did that one night at the club. But I did two --- one in the evening and one at night, (concerts).

566.t: A writer's family in France; first trips in 1962, 1973 and 1975
566.s: She mentions another French family headed by a writer, met at George Wein's 1975 festival. She dates her first French trip to 1973 for Black and Blue, after the 1962 blues festival.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: That is the sweetest family I ever met. And then there is another family there. This fellow is a writer, Mr. Drachu s.

566.t: The 1972-73 Black and Blue session with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner
566.s: After the Basie tribute Stanley Dance arranged, she was in France five days later, touring for Monestier and recording 'Helen Comes Back' with Jay McShann and Milt Buckner. Dance praises McShann's range beyond blues piano.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: Yes. Well, I didn't know anything about him until then. You know, when I came over and Stanley (Dance) came and had me do this Basie thing in '72.

566.t: Monestier and Tamadjian: touring and studios of Black and Blue
566.s: Monestier and his partner Tamadjian promote tours and concerts together. Humes sometimes rode the bus with the musicians. She notes Monestier's pretended lack of understanding and cannot say whether the studio is in Bordeaux or Paris.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: But Monestier, he never could understand nobody. I think he was like that just because he didn't want to understand.

566.t: Hugues Panassie and his wife follow her tours
566.s: Panassie and his wife Natalie always turned up wherever she sang in France, and Panassie marveled that even young people loved her and wanted her to keep singing. The text is broken by an out-of-order page.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: Yes. They always come where I was. And I'd go somewhere and I'd look up and the first thing I'd see would be him and his wife. And he said, 'you know Helen I just can't understand it. It just seems like these people just love you so and they don't never want you to stop singing.' He said, 'even the…

566.t: Sir Charles Thompson: plans to work together
566.s: Humes is alive and in Zurich and plans to use Sir Charles Thompson at the Cookery. He is sometimes touchy with the band, she advises him to just go along, and she notes people must go to Europe to get big.
566.q: Yeah. And I told him, I said, now just go on and let the boys say whatever they want to say, and you go in and grin and bare it and just fall in line, you know.

566.t: Live recording at Montreux and European applause
566.s: Humes thought the Montreux live album was her worst and noisy, but she likes the sound of European audiences applauding and standing for her.
566.q: Yes, that was the worse one I've ever made. Well, they made it live out there.

566.t: First trip to Japan with Teddy Wilson, Milt Hinton and Shelly Manne
566.s: She went to Japan in August 1980 with a group including Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Milt Hinton, Shelly Manne and Lockjaw. Audiences went crazy, Shirley Silver carried her bags, and she did three concerts in eight days.
566.q: No I didn't take a group but a group went. They had Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, and Milt Harry Hinton, Shelly Mann, / Edison. Lockjaw was there.

566.t: Two weeks at Ronnie Scott's in London
566.s: From Japan she went via New York to London for two weeks at Ronnie Scott's with English backing musicians, and saw Max Jones. She says she is not as close to the English as to the French.
566.q: Then I left there and come right on back to New York and went on to London.

566.t: France within a month: Dr. Chavron and the 'Helen Comes Back' session
566.s: A month later she was in France for her first time in that way, meeting Dr. Chavron, touring for Monestier and recording for Black and Blue with Milt Buckner and Jay McShann, who was in good form.
566.q: Yeah, he was in good form that day.

760.t: Jam session in Oklahoma City and young European jazz fans
760.s: He recalls Ann Cooper at a jam session, then describes the teenage audiences and packed jazz clubs he found in England and Liverpool.
760.q: No, playing good trumpet playing like her, because she played just like, you'd never think it was a girl. And one thing about her, they used to have jam sessions during those times, and we used to play places, and when the fellows get off, they used to jam. Like we played Oklahoma City, and the…

760.t: Concerts, a Copenhagen club and television in Europe
760.s: The tour is mostly concerts, with four nights in a new Copenhagen club and television appearances in Germany, Denmark and England.
760.q: Well, most, all our playing was concerts, all except in Denmark. We played concerts in Denmark but in Copenhagen they opened up a club, a jazz club, a new jazz club, followed by the name of Andy, Hendrix, Carl. And we played in this club four nights. Oh yeah. Yeah. But all the rest of it was…

760.t: Crowds in Stockholm and Scotland following Armstrong
760.s: A sold-out Stockholm concert hall, enthusiastic audiences everywhere, and Scottish musicians who make them feel at home.
760.q: We played Stockholm, Sweden, and we had so many people at this kind of sector. The fire marshal wouldn't leave anybody else in. And this is one of the largest places that I played in. It had about five balconies to this. That's why they give all these ballets and all the big concerts, different…

760.t: London arrival, Ken Colyer's club and sitting in with British bands
760.s: The crowd and brass band at the London station, a jam session at Colyer's club, and sitting in with Alan Yates, Rudy Marcellus and Chris Barber.
760.q: Well, yeah, they was all hollering, George Lewis, you know, and they had signs and they played. So when we got in, when they got to playing, when the ship landed, they came on the ship and it happened to be Chris Barbara and his band. And so anyway, well, that was fine. And we talked with them and…

760.t: Chris Barber's hit record, and not reaching Ireland or France
760.s: The Barber group's record is a hit in America and England; the tour did not stop in Ireland and the band did not go to France.
760.q: They're very nice fellows. And one thing about this record that they made, this of Bish years, this PT4, this thing is sweeping the country. That's all they're playing around. New York. New York. And oh, it's a big hit over here and it is in England and it's really good in England, you know. And of…

760.t: Paris and other countries he did not visit
760.s: He learns Paris was an easy day trip and lists the countries visited and missed.
760.q: Yeah. And I said, well, he said, yeah, he said, you don't take it no time, he said, to go to Paris from here, he said, go in the morning and come back in the evening. He said, if you had two or three days, he said, I'd take you and go on the boat train where they, on this boat, you can take your…

760.t: Contracts limited the itinerary; warm receptions and comparison with Armstrong
760.s: Contract arrangements kept them from more countries, but Swedish and Danish welcomes, honorary club memberships and London concerts followed, and some thought his band better than Armstrong's.
760.q: The airport. Well, what it was, we had a chance to go to all those places, to Italy, France, Vienna, all those places we had a chance to go to after we got there. But trouble was, when they signed the contracts, they had made an arrangement for George to play three weeks with Kaye in Germany, you…

760.t: European fans' knowledge of New Orleans jazz history
760.s: Fans abroad know the old bands, photographs and books, and reminded him of forgotten New Orleans musicians; he mentions Henrik in Denmark.
760.q: Yeah, well that's what they thought, but the most thing it was, I think it was because they said it was traditional. Yeah, they liked that. And they liked that, you see. And they really liked the band and all the fellas, they liked Jim, they liked everybody that was in the band. And everywhere we…

760.t: Hotels, food, sightseeing and concert halls
760.s: His views on hotels and heating, food and restaurants, the sights he visited, and the halls they played.
760.q: Well, I tell you, the hotels over there are very nice and a lot of them are real modern. It's like the big hotels here and the only thing about the hotels over there, the people over there don't believe in too much heat. You know, that's one thing. It'd be cold out there and they have that heat on…

760.t: European jazz musicians as imitators, and the Baden-Baden TV show
760.s: European players call themselves imitators of the originators; he describes a blues singer named Barrow and the Vienna guitarist at the Baden-Baden show.
760.q: Yeah, he had the best band for many, many years. He had a real good band. And I'll tell you what I would, what I would like to get back to, uh, England again. For him. For, for. For one thing I wanted, I wanted to, you know, the musicians to know that how much these, these musicians over in Europe,…

760.t: Foreign customs: driving, unarmed police and autograph crowds
760.s: He remarks on driving on the left, bicycles, courteous police, and fans waiting in the snow for autographs.
760.q: Wrong side of the street. You know, it always looked like it was going to run into something and the car would be coming, it looked like it was heading into the car, you know. And a lot of times Jim would say, whoo, you know. It's quite a while to, you know, to get used to it. And it always looked…

85.t: The telegram offer from Willie Lewis in Paris
85.s: Carter received a telegram from Willie Lewis in 1935 offering him a job in Paris.
85.q: Well, it was tendered by my having received a telegram from Willie Lewis, actually, in Paris, offering me the job, you know, if I would like to come to Paris and play with his orchestra. I don’t know how long it took me to think it over, but I decided I would like to do it, and I did.

85.t: Why he went to Europe, and the word expatriate
85.s: Carter says he wanted to see another culture, went for almost three years, and meant to return only for a visit.
85.q: It might have been, but not necessarily. But I guess we all, you know, think of going to faraway places at some time in our lives, and whether it was Europe or anyplace else. But it would probably have been the place I would be more interested than any other place at that time.

85.t: Leonard Feather and arranging for the BBC in London
85.s: Feather cabled him to write for the BBC radio staff band; he wrote about three arrangements a week and could not get a permit to play.
85.q: That’s right. We had never met, and I got a cable from Leonard, asking me if I would be interested in coming to London [England] to work for the BBC [British Broadcasting Company] as an arranger. That was very interesting to me. I corresponded with him and answered, of course, in the affirmative,…

85.t: Treatment in Europe and the Hippodrome concert
85.s: Carter was received with respect, and his one permitted public playing was a concert at the Hippodrome.
85.q: Well, of course, I did, but what I did was exposed to a much broader audience there, and my coming seemed to have created, in some circles, considered to be newsworthy and noteworthy, you know. I was treated with a great respect and given a very handsome welcome. I had a very, very nice tenure…

85.t: Work permit limits and the Royal Academy of Music
85.s: Having to leave England every three months stopped Carter from starting formal study at the Academy.
85.q: Yes. I had intended undergoing some studies there. As a matter of fact, I went to the Royal Academy of Music, and had an interview with a professor . . . what was his name? Oh, boy. I had it on the tip of my tongue, and now it escapes me. But anyway, the problem was that I had to leave the country…

85.t: Rosamond Johnson's help with his first film work
85.s: Rosamond Johnson in London helped him as he prepared a British film score.
85.q: Well, I must certainly say that I did receive help from him. I wish I’d been able to have spent more time with him, but he was very busy and so was I. But he was in London at the time. Just what he was doing there, I don’t remember. But he was a very, very talented man. Oh, boy, there isn’t enough…

85.t: The European musicians and the Scheveningen international band
85.s: Carter names the players in his European units and says the interracial, international band was about getting the best players.
85.q: Chisholm, Chisholm. Chisholm. But he is a name that still would be recognized today. The others, I don’t think there would be too many known. Bertie King and, oh, gee whiz. Oh, I can’t remember. York DeSousa [phonetic] at the piano, and Robert Monmarchet [phonetic], who was a [phonetic] drummer…

85.t: News of American swing reaching Europe
85.s: Carter heard records and knew of Goodman's success, but felt little had developed in the meantime.
85.q: Well, we were hearing records that were getting there; I don’t know how much later than having been released in America, but that’s about it, you know. It wasn’t . . . as a matter of fact, during that particular period, I don’t think there was too much, actually, too much development, as you call…

85.t: Deciding to come home from Europe
85.s: There was no big reason, he simply wanted to go home for a while.
85.q: Well, it was really more than that. It was just wanting to come back home for a while and, as I said, when I came back, I had intended returning to Europe, you know. But I don’t know. There was no big compelling reason, just sort of . . . just a matter of change and come home for a bit and go back,…

85.t: Playing society dance music with Willie Lewis at Chez Florence
85.s: The Lewis band played show tunes and melody for a jet-set crowd, with few Carter arrangements.
85.q: Well, Willie Lewis was a clarinetist and saxophonist who had gone to Europe with the Sam Wooding Orchestra. So, you know, it was sort of as a jazz orchestra, but we played mostly society music, because we played in a club called the Chez Florence and mostly

85.s: Carter found Django quiet and shy and describes his playing as a revelation despite his injured hand.
85.q: Not much. There wasn’t much to know about Django. He was very quiet. He had very little to say. That’s being redundant, isn’t it? [Berger laughs.] But anyway, he was also maybe a little on the shy side, and maybe that was more because being around American musicians and not speaking English, and we…

26.t: Europe in 1933 to be told separately
26.s: Greer says the 1933 European tour is big and should go in another segment; Crouch moves on.
26.q: Let's put that in another segment. That European was big. One of the biggest. That's one of the biggies.

26.t: Sophie Tucker, Lady Mountbatten and the invitation to London
26.s: After a visit by Sophie Tucker, the band gets booked to London in 1933.
26.q: She was big, so one night she come up there with Lady Mountbatten, Lord Louis Mountbatten was a big man, an Englishman, he was Lord Louis Mountbatten. During the war he was in charge of a whole fleet, so he was a big man, one of the biggest and she was a cousin of the Queen, Lady Mountbatten was.

26.t: Jack Hilton's imitation band in London
26.s: Greer hears Jack Hilton's band copying the records but lacking the solos.
26.q: '33. They had all the advertisement on the buses, the big two-story buses, advertised like a circus. At that time they had a band in London named Jack Hilton. He was like the Paul Whiteman that was here, so this cat he had a band, we had a couple of days before we opened in London, so I was riding…

26.t: Opening day at the Palladium and the Prince of Wales arrives
26.s: Backstage before the Palladium, the Prince of Wales interrupts a singer's act.
26.q: We opened up at the Palladium, I'll never forget it. We did, they call it first and second house, and that's like a matinee in the afternoon. It's really the afternoon about three or four o'clock so we closed the first half of the program.

26.s: List of English towns and countries on the 1933 tour.
26.q: We stayed -- oh, we played the Palladium, we played a concert at the Elephant Castle, a big concert hall, we played another concert in Margate, England, and then we played Liverpool, played Blackpool and we played Birmingham, oh, about a month and a half, all over England.

26.s: Greer says Europeans were more enthusiastic and tells of 300 girls singing Happy Birthday.
26.q: Yeah. They were -- it's hard to say, but they were more enthusiastic for the simple reason -- it wasn't like in America, like you can go hear anybody you want. It was a rarity, and they were so overjoyed to see us in person and hear them in person that they were more enthusiastic.

26.t: Hotels and flags on the Continental tour
26.s: Irving Mills booked the best hotels, and the American flag flew.
26.q: We stayed in the biggest hotels, we stayed in the biggest hotels, baby. I'm tell you like it is. We stayed in the biggest hotels. Every hotel we stayed in, because Irving Mills had our accommodations in front in the biggest hotels in every country. They fly -- like they fly for the dignitary the…

26.t: Lord Beaverbrook's party and the future King at the piano
26.s: The band plays Beaverbrook's party; the Prince of Wales grabs Duke at the piano.
26.q: But let me tell you a little incident. This will kill you. So while I was in London in 1933, so Lord Beaverbrook, he's a Canadian, but he owns all the newspapers. You may have heard of him. He's big, big there. He would throw him a party so he throws this party at his mansion, you know, and

26.t: Drinking and drumming with the Prince of Wales
26.s: Greer teaches the Prince the Charleston and calls him 'the Wale'.
26.q: is this big magnum of champagne in front of everybody and a bottle of Scotch -- bottle of brandy. One sitting there by me. I look at this fellow, I said, little taste, everything fine so now this cat sitting down on the floor he had one of them brandy snifters, big things, he's going with it. I…

26.t: 'I was there': pride in representing Black America
26.s: Greer speaks of carrying the dignity of the American Negro.
26.q: I hear the cats talking about, we -- I say this, because I'm the only one in a position to speak now, because I'm one of the few-- I'm the only living original member of the band. We carried the flag, the American flag and the prestige for my people. I hear all these loudmouths talking about so and…

26.t: Don Byas and Django Reinhardt with the band
26.s: Greer recalls hiring Don Byas as guest in Europe and bringing Django Reinhardt to Carnegie Hall.
26.q: We went to Europe and Duke hired Don Byas just as a guest soloist. He played -- what's that song -- "Oh, Danny Boy." In four different tempos. Kill you. Don Byas, he was my running mate. He'd say, man -- he lived in Europe. "Man, you --

86.t: Appreciation of jazz abroad and the expatriates
86.s: Edison discusses jazz and spirituals in Europe and Japan and why Ben Webster and others stayed in Europe.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: It sure is. And now, the spirituals are beginning to really be so popular in Europe. They have a guy named Willie Liezo over in Switzerland, all he books over there is gospel singers. The people over there love it, gospel churches, they love it. You couldn’t even sell them over here. Over there,…

86.t: Traveling as a soloist with local rhythm sections
86.s: He describes European pickup groups of uneven quality and how he adapts to their keys.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: No, I never have been surprised in that way. I have been surprised most of the time if they could play. Because travelling as a soloist as I do, you’re at the mercy of whoever they get for you. In Europe, I’ve played with some groups that knew nothing but the blues. So, I’ve played the blues fast,…

86.t: Istanbul, Kuwait and the 1976 tour with Benny Carter
86.s: He recalls the Bicentennial tour with Benny Carter and Morroe Berger.
86.ch: Travels, horn and views on new music
86.q: I had a good time there in Kuwait. Yeah, I had a nice time in Kuwait. And I had a nice time in Istanbul. I went over there with Benny Carter in 1976 I think it was…the Bicentennial. I was with your father.

86.t: Bicentennial State Department tour: Istanbul, Iran, Pakistan
86.s: Edison tells of being picked with Benny Carter's group to tour the Middle East, seeing Istanbul, Ankara, Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz and Karachi.
86.q: So during the Bicentennial, the American government, they asked -- five musicians were chosen, I was one of the five, to do a tour of the Middle East, you know, and Cleopatra has always been one of my favorite rulers, you know. She was in an age where I think it was absolutely just fabulous back in…

86.t: Representing America with jazz: the band and embassy concerts
86.s: Edison names the tour band and says they played short embassy-hall concerts and were treated like VIPs.
86.q: the Johnny Carson Show. And a girl singer, who I can't think of her name now, but she was a good singer. Benny Carter recommended her, so there's no doubt about when he recommends somebody. They have talent, you know.

86.t: Jordan: King Hussein's family, Irbid and Jerash
86.s: The band played two concerts in Jordan, a make-up date in Irbid after Benny Carter fell ill, and visited Jerash.
86.q: In fact, they are the ones that sponsored the concert in Jordan, yeah, his wife, and the concert -- we had to do two concerts, it was so crowded in both of them. Just absolutely

86.t: Ambassadors drawn out by jazz concerts
86.s: At embassies, diplomats who ignored invitations came to hear Benny Carter's band, and the group was received warmly abroad.
86.q: See, we wouldn't play but an hour a night, you know. And every day, we'd have dinner with the ambassador and his family and in -- let's see, in one place there, the ambassador, American ambassador, he had been trying to get a rendezvous with most of the political figures there -- I think it was in…

86.t: Jazz respected abroad but not at home
86.s: Edison and Dance remark that jazz is taken seriously and subsidized abroad but not in the United States.
86.q: That was -- it's amazing why, you know, that jazz is appreciated so much in other countries and it's not appreciated here.

86.t: Sightseeing in Egypt: pyramids, Tutankhamen and the Nile
86.s: Edison toured historical sites alone, saw the Tutankhamen treasure, and dined on the Nile before the Alexandria concert.
86.q: I went to the Egyptian museum, right behind the Cairo Hilton Hotel. You could walk right out the back and walk right across the street, was the museum, you know? And --

86.s: He likes sightseeing in Paris, Denmark and London.
86.ch: Travels, horn and views on new music
86.q: No, I like to see, I like to look. As I said before, I’m so blessed because a lot of places I never thought I’d see, that I read about in school, now I’m right there looking at a historical place you would never think that you would be walking in Notre Dame in England, walking in the Louvre in…

527.t: First European tour: cities and North Africa
527.s: Cities played in Europe, and a Tunisian date where the sidemen played before Hampton arrived.
527.q: Aw man, it was great! Fantastic. We didn’t play in London because there was a union problem there, so we didn’t get to play there, but we played in Paris, Berlin, Stockholm and Copenhagen and Helsinki. We didn’t play Rome, but we played there for like three months. We played North Africa.

527.t: The 1964 European tour with the Hall quartet and To Sweden, With Love
527.s: Free-form quartet with Steve Swallow and Pete La Roca, the Swedish folk song album, and Monty Kay as booker.
527.q: The bassist was Steve Swallow, and the drummer was Pete La Roca. Pete La Roca and Steve Swallow played so good together. The group would, what I would call, played sort of freely. We played tunes, but everybody was free to do whatever they wanted to do on the tunes. We had skeleton arrangements,…

527.t: Americans in the Austrian radio band
527.s: Jimmy Woode, a Kent State trombone section, Bill Dobbins, and three or four years with the orchestra.
527.q: He used to play with Duke’s band. He was on the bass, and then when the group was first organized, the whole trombone section was taken from Kent State, like a year or two after that riot happened out there where a few people got killed. The band came over to play at the Montreux Jazz Festival, and…

527.t: Returning to play in America each summer, Clifford Jordan and local rhythm sections
527.s: Summer work in New York with Jimmy Heath, then Clifford Jordan, versus playing with weak local groups in Europe.
527.q: I would say like for the first two years, I just stayed over there, but then after that, I started coming over – or maybe the first year – I started coming over each summer,

527.t: Effect of living abroad on his outlook, and loneliness at first
527.s: Every place has pluses and minuses; he felt isolated from friends at first but musicians were friendly.
527.q: Yeah, to a point, because if you just stay here, people here think everything is rotating around the United States, but that’s not true. In Austria, people think everything is rotating around Austria too [laughs]. They think if it didn’t happen in Vienna, it wasn’t worth happening. But, if you live…

527.t: Concert opportunities in France, Austria and England
527.s: Houses of Culture in France, small concerts in Austria and Germany, and a yearly two-week English tour.
527.q: Yeah, I have opportunities to play concerts there. France has an Office of Culture, and they spend a lot of money on concerts, jazz and everything else. I have an agent there. I play about three or four concerts there in what’s called Houses of Culture. It’s not just music, but whatever has to do…

527.t: The Vienna jazz scene and subsidized clubs
527.s: Bookings by phone, Porgy and Bess and Jazzland supported by the city, and Ray Brown's visit.
527.q: People call me up, and that’s it. We don’t have a booking agent over there. They either call me or call Harry Sokal, the tenor saxophone player. Harry plays also with a group called The Vienna Art Orchestra that comes over here maybe once every year or so.

527.t: Fritz Pauer, the band's director, and the year of the move
527.s: Pauer was pianist, Johannes Fehring musical director, and Farmer became a resident in 1968.
527.q: It says ’68 because what happened was that I still had my place over here, but I had sublet it, and in ’68, I let it go. That’s when I started saying that’s the time I really became a resident in Europe.

527.t: The Vienna jazz competition and the radio jazz band offer
527.s: Friedrich Gulda's competition with Cannonball and others as judges led to an offer from the Vienna radio's jazz orchestra, which later turned commercial.
527.q: There’s a classic pianist named Friedrich Gulda, and I ran into him in Berlin. On my off night, I went to a concert he was playing. He was playing a concert and had Ron Carter and Tootie Heath. The first part of the concert he’d play classic Mozart and all that, and then the second half was jazz. I…

527.t: Returning to Europe with Mulligan and asking for more pay after the tour
527.s: Reception in Europe improved by 1958 because people knew his records; he asked Mulligan for more money after the gig and Norman Granz agreed.
527.q: No, the first time I returned to Europe was with Mulligan say like in ’58, ’59 or something like that, just before we organized the Jazztet.

89.t: Berlin reception and the route through Europe
89.s: The show was well received in Berlin despite objections, then toured Scandinavia, Central Europe, Spain and Russia before the group left the show in Paris.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: Received wonderfully well. The people thought it was great. Some of the Germans still had their effects of World War I in their minds and they objected to us being there because they said they had so much trouble with the Senegalese during the war and they didn't want to see any more black people.…

89.t: Hearing European musicians and pioneering jazz abroad
89.s: European groups tried to play jazz but were unfamiliar with it, so Wooding's big stage band was a pioneering novelty.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: Oh, my goodness, yes. Jazz, you see -- they tried to play jazz and they knew nothing of it. And what I heard was their music and I was impressed -- particularly the gypsies.

89.t: Which country understood jazz, and flopping in London
89.s: France understood jazz best because black musicians lived in Paris; the band flopped at Holborn Empire in London for being too classy.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: longer than anyone else, because the black musicians went to France. They didn't go to Germany. They didn't go to Russia. They didn't go to -- later they spread into Sweden and Germany, but France was the headquarters. All the black musicians of Europe went to Paris. The Frenchmen were really…

89.t: Back from Europe: the classy Sam Wooding vaudeville act
89.s: The band returned feeling special, formed a concert-style vaudeville act, and he praises Wooding as composer and arranger still working at 82.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: Well, naturally, we were youngsters and we were highly impressed with the people and the attitude and the mannerisms of Europeans and we sort of took on some of that and we assumed some of that air. And we didn't fall back into the same groove that we had been in when we left, because we were more…

89.t: From the broadcast to the European engagement
89.s: Letters and vaudeville followed, and agent Arthur Lyons heard of the band, leading to the Europe tour.
89.ch: Recollections of bands, dances and tours
89.q: Well, we naturally went back to the Nist but so many people heard us and we got letters and we did vaudeville. Then we went into vaudeville around -- in and around New York, not too far so we could come back and make our engagement at the Nist every night. But this agent had heard

89.t: Admission prices, packed houses and length of the tour
89.s: Audiences paid five dollars to see them in packed houses, in what he calls the first large band in Europe; the tour lasted two years.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: Yes. Those days people were paying an unheard of price of $5.00 admission, you know, and that's 40, 50 years ago, $5.00 admission, but this was an unusual thing. Don't forget, it was from America and they'd pay $5.00 to hear it. Ordinarily, they'd just pay $1.00 to hear their own attractions. That…

89.s: Danish women were so taken with the American musicians that a cabaret owner banned them.
89.q: show in Copenhagen and the show went on back to Germany, but we stayed there a while, trying to settle our affairs and deciding what we were going to do.

89.t: Organizing the Sam Wooding revue for Europe and the voyage
89.s: Agent Arthur Lyons organized a 53-person Negro revue with Ellington's music, which rehearsed on the boat.
89.ch: Europe and South America with Sam Wooding
89.q: Yeah, well, if you wish to speak of that -- if you want to get through more incidents in '25, between '25 and '30, including Europe.

89.t: Madagascar, Dar es Salaam and Morocco
89.s: After a beauty contest at Zanzibar the band went to Madagascar, Dar es Salaam, Nairobi and Morocco, where he bought souvenirs.
89.q: No, from that section, Zanzibar. From Zanzibar -- Zanzibar's quite a good size island. And we went from there to the Island of Madagascar which is the largest island in the world, I believe -- or almost the largest, next to Greenland, I believe. They call it Malagash. They speak French there.…

114.s: He returned because the record was a hit and he decided he had every right to be in America.
114.q: Well I came because the record was a hit, and they kind of convinced me, they said go over there and make some money and then come back. I says okay, that’s what I did. Then when I got over here I says it’s ridiculous for me to run away from the place where I’m born, I’m raised, I have every right…

114.t: Living with Uncle Louie in Paris without working
114.s: He did not work in Paris, living in his uncle's apartment near the Eiffel Tower; his uncle worked for the American government.
114.ch: Alcohol, Paris and the hit record
114.q: No, no. I didn't work at all. I didn't have to because my uncle, they had a large one- floor apartment. My uncle and my Aunt Flowers [phonetic sp.], and had a maid. I mean, it had maid quarters upstairs. I mean, it was really. And we were right there. We'd open up the -- the ­ - the blinds -- not…

114.t: His mother's schooling and polish; Paris widened his view
114.s: His mother wanted him polished, not a clown, and Paris in the late 1940s confirmed that people are the same everywhere.
114.q: school because my mother told me, she said my aunt's husband grabbed her and tried to do things to her, to seduce her. And her mother got pissed off thinking it was her fault. See? So now I can relate to all these women being abused and things because my mother's mother's sister's husband tried to…

114.s: He has played everywhere but India and China, visited Gorée and Eastern Europe, and found it sad returning after Dizzy died.
114.q: Oh yeah. Everywhere except India. Who would want to go to India, and mainland China, yeah mainland China, who wants to go there? But people are the same all over the world, no matter where you go, they are the same. And people want the same thing. Like they want to be able to make a living, they…

114.s: Being treated with respect in France was a revelation; he was angry at the system, not individuals.
114.ch: Alcohol, Paris and the hit record
114.q: Yeah, I look, I said, "Damn! That was something," you know. And I never will forget, I used to write home to my mother. I addressed it, USA. I used to write, "USA, Land of [indiscernible]".

114.t: Dizzy's quintet repertoire and personnel; Dizzy loved everywhere
114.s: The quintet played Dizzy's music with a stable lineup, and Dizzy was recognized in airports worldwide.
114.q: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Play [indiscernible], you know, "Umbrella Man", [indiscernible], you know, "One Old [indiscernible]". Yeah. Was nice.

114.s: People everywhere respond to music and to a gentleman who tries their language.
114.q: You know what? You know what? People are responsive to the music, but most of all, people are responsive to you especially if you try to say something in their tongue and -- and act like a gentleman. I mean, you know, you know, act -- act civil. Act nice. People are nice all over the world. You…

114.t: Living in Paris and leaving America over racism
114.s: He was not going to return from France because of racism, as in his joking letters home.
114.ch: Race and racism on the road
114.q: True story, right honey? So and it became a big seller. So then one day I’m in New York, because I wasn’t going to come back, I was living in France then, in Paris. I wasn’t going to come back because I never will forget I used to write things to my mother and I used to say things like, I shouldn’t…

464.t: First trip to Europe in 1967 and recording with the Metropole Orchestra
464.s: He goes to Europe with guitarist Attila Zoller, then records in Holland, first using Tom McIntosh's arrangements, then his own.
464.ch: Marshall Brown, Ellington and first trips abroad
464.q: …was a very fine guitarist. He died a number of years ago. He was a very fine guitarist. He was a gypsy and he played with Herbie Mann before I was with Herbie Mann. That’s when I met him, actually, you know. We liked the way each other played and he invited me to go to Europe with him. We had gigs…

464.s: Owens says many left because of segregation, and those who stayed often turned to substance abuse.
464.q: Most of the musicians that moved to Europe—that’s why they moved to Europe, because of the segregation in American and how that affected them musically. You know, what they could not do. If the ones who stayed didn’t move to Europe, then they got substance abuse problems to kind of bury all of that…

464.t: Sound advice to Billy Taylor and Freddie Hubbard; the 1989 Latin America tour
464.s: He advises other State Department artists about pianos and sound, then tours South America in 1989 with Giulio Capiozzo and Seabreeze.
464.ch: Touring: State Department, Senegal and Dizzy
464.q: Most definitely. At the same time, as time went on, Billy Taylor was going to do that tour the next year, only he was starting in Pakistan and working back toward Morocco. I told Billy Taylor, “First, you should make them crate a piano for you. A Steinway piano, just like Horwitz would do if he was…

464.t: Senegal in 1980: Club Med and the Goree Island concert
464.s: His quartet and family go to the independence festival, where he plays to 35,000 people alongside Dizzy Gillespie.
464.ch: Touring: State Department, Senegal and Dizzy
464.q: Again, we got wonderful reviews form the various embassies and the chief officers of the embassies, and the performing people who set up the concerts. In between those tours I did a number of concerts, Morocco with the group, I went back to Senegal. I was in Senegal the first time in 1980. I took…

464.t: Why 'Jimmy Owens Plus'; Europe and the 1981 State Department tour
464.s: He explains the group name, then describes the six-week 1981 tour, canceled Israel concerts and his sound-equipment demands.
464.ch: Touring: State Department, Senegal and Dizzy
464.q: Okay, you know so, Jimmy Owens Plus, first of all, the title of my group comes from the fact that the plus was always something special that I was performing with. It could be Jimmy Owens Plus the Rochester Philharmonic Orchestra, or the Symphony of the New World Orchestra, Jimmy Owens Plus the Rod…

464.t: Billy Taylor's Frost show, the New York Jazz Sextet and Jimmy Owens Plus
464.s: With Frost show days off he books college concerts with his own groups, the Sextet and then recordings in Europe in 1972.
464.ch: Learning from bandleaders; teaching and Frost years
464.q: Frost show that I didn’t miss much of that. But, when we started to work sometimes three days, I found myself going to colleges on the days off. I was booked for those particular things; I had a manager that was booking me and my group, Jimmy Owens Plus, from 1969. That was Anne Summers Management.…

464.t: Jazz, narcotics and racism, then and in Europe
464.s: Owens says drug use among jazz musicians has declined as racism has eased, citing segregation on the road. He says European musicians now have the problems America had earlier.
464.ch: Views on the music and its business
464.q: Oh most definitely. It’s gotten better because life in America has gotten better. As we pinpointed racism a little more and made things better for African American people, narcotics stopped a little bit in the jazz musician — a lot I should say — in the jazz musician community. It’s really…

464.t: The 1968 Dizzy Gillespie Reunion Tour of Europe
464.s: He puts together the big band, surprises Dizzy with 'Happy Birthday' instead of 'Things to Come', and lists the personnel.
464.ch: Touring: State Department, Senegal and Dizzy
464.q: getting ready to play. He’s playing one song with his group. We waited until that song was over and we marched up the roadway playing “Night In Tunisia” as a march. (Scats melody of “Night In Tunisia”) He heard this, and we had a drummer playing with us too, he heard this and said, “What is that?”…

677.t: First European tour solos and records
677.s: On the 1933 trip his solos were Trees, Rose of the Rio Grande and Sheik; band made records there and acceptance of sweeter music followed.
677.q: Yeah, that type of stuff. Of course, we played all this other, you know, too, also. And everybody had a solo practically in every piece. It was one solo of somebody one after another. So, it was strictly a solo band almost, plus a few together numbers.

677.t: The 1933 European trip and playing for the Prince of Wales
677.s: The trip was hectic with theaters and private parties for the Prince of Wales and Lord Beaverbrook; Brown was seasick on the boat.
677.ch: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group
677.q: Oh, well that was a hectic trip because we were pioneering, according to certain people. And it entailed quite a few little incidents. We would play in a theater and then play a dance -- go to play a dance or a party -- mostly a party -- private party.

677.t: Senegal festival and State Department tours
677.s: Brown describes the tour in the Middle East, South America and a festival in Senegal at the president's invitation.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Yes, we did a State tour in the Middle East and went through South America and, oh, one in -- we went to a music festival in Africa.

677.t: Embassy visits and meeting local people
677.s: Embassy engagements were catering to the head man, with monsoons in Ceylon and a sitar player, and little contact with locals.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Yes, we did some, and -- but, you see, mostly they catered to the head man. We were just there really. You get that feeling it's -- you're just invited because the head man was invited, so I didn't -- it was nice, but there wasn't too much activity, and it's strange -- everything was strange. And…

677.t: European audiences who know your solos
677.s: Danes and Swedes studied recordings; he mentions the Netherlands and Ben Webster in Amsterdam.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Oh, yes, they really study. They know everything you're going -- they know all of your solos. They'll hum along or remind you of this solo that you played in such and such a piece and were very nice.

677.t: In Turkey when Kennedy was assassinated
677.s: The band was in Ankara when the agent woke them with the news, and the tour was cut off.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Well, we were -- we had gone to bed in this hotel, and our agent, government agent came around and knocked on the door and said, 'We're leaving. They've assassinated our President.' So tomorrow, the next day we got together and left. No, it was that next day or two days, couple of days…

677.t: Slippery Horn and other dates on the England trip
677.s: Brown had never heard that Slippery Horn was named for him and recalls two theaters and many private parties.
677.ch: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group
677.q: We played two theaters, which the names have slipped me. And as I say again, so many -- we played so many private parties and things that the bookkeeping got all mixed up as to how many we really had played. But they did very well on that trip.

677.s: In Paris the audience resented a girl singer humming sophisticated pieces and wanted jazz.
677.q: Most of them. The only time I ever heard the audience resent what was going on was in France, in Paris one time. They -- Ellington had gotten to the place where he was playing these very sophisticated things, and well, the audience just resented it completely and starting booing. And especially…

19.t: Paramount Theatre with Jacquet's big band, then sailing to Europe without the trio
19.s: After Christmas at the Paramount, Sarah, her husband, valet and Malachi sail on the Liberte because the budget cannot carry Crosby and Freeman.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: We finished the tour... I think it started around October, and we finished it around the middle of December, after which we started preparing to go into the Paramount Theatre with Illinois Jacquet's big band, at that time which was a very good band, including people like Budd Johnson and a host of…

19.t: Rehearsing with a Melody Maker-winning British band and touring England
19.s: The poll-winning band is eager but young and underprepared in the postwar period, and they tour many English towns.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: Anyway, after that, we had rehearsal with this band who had won the Melody Maker poll over there as being the band of the year. The Melody Maker is the English equivalent to Downbeat in the United States. I don't remember the name of this bandleader, but he was so happy to be working with Sarah…

19.t: Wales, Scotland and Glasgow pianist John Scott Henderson
19.s: A Glasgow pianist who knew of Malachi writes ahead and meets him at the station, showing him the town.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: went to Wales -- Cardiff, Wales, and some other little town in Wales. Finally, we closed the tour with a tour to Scotland, where I... I had a very nice time in Scotland.

19.t: Unheated buses and hotels; Royal Albert Hall
19.s: January in Britain with no bus heat and sixpence-meter heaters, which he believes helped bring on arthritis, ends with a packed Royal Albert Hall concert.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: We were in Glasgow a couple of days, and then we went to a couple of other cities in Scotland -- I can't remember right now. But anyway, it all turned out to be quite an experience, because first of all, this was in January. And being used to

19.s: The train boards the ferry at Dover, and in Paris the problem is the language rather than the money.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: everybody was very regretful about leaving. But our next engagement was in Paris. So we had our final goodbyes and everything to London, and we crossed the English Channel to Paris. At that particular time, you caught the train in London, and in Dover the train was boarded onto the boat, and the…

19.t: Playing behind the curtain in a swank Paris club
19.s: Sarah is the only visible performer while the band led by a Martinique-born flautist plays behind the curtain, making cues a challenge.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: But we were in Paris, and we opened at a very swanky club called the La Darpdor(?) -- I think the translation is The Golden Crepe. Anyway, it was just so high class. They had suits of armor around, and all kinds of drapes -- it looked like some room in a big castle somewhere. But we had a big band…

19.t: Jazz at the Philharmonic, Sugar Ray Robinson's club and the Chez Sassy
19.s: After work musicians gather at Sugar Ray Robinson's club, and a Paris club is named after Sarah.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: During that particular time, Jazz at the Philharmonic came over with Oscar Peterson and Ray Brown, Ella Fitzgerald. At that particular time, the boxer, Sugar Ray Robinson, had a club over there. This is where we all congregated after we got off of work. It turned out to be a very happy time.

19.t: London welcome and a BBC broadcast that starts when the BBC wants
19.s: Greeted like royalty, they arrive early for the 8 o'clock broadcast and learn British radio starts when it pleases.
19.ch: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
19.q: Anyway, we arrived at London and we were greeted just like what we felt like was royalty, because there were people waiting at the train station, and we were treated very well, taken to the hotels and given every courtesy. The London media and the agents and everything... Everything was just…

22.t: Replacements, trip to London and Satanic Blues
22.s: After Edwards entered the Army in 1918, Christian joined and the band took jazz to London and wrote Satanic Blues.
22.ch: Band in New York and London
22.q: Well, there's a little more story to that, Dave. Well, why don't you tell it to us? Well, in 1918, when the draft came on, Edwards was put into the Army. I came to New Orleans, and I picked up another great man and a good musician, Emil Christ.

22.t: Return from Europe, decline of the band and attempted reunion
22.s: Records sold worldwide; return to New York in 1920, New Orleans in 1925, and a thwarted 1936 reunion.
22.q: uh well you would you like me to take the part where I come back to New York and we uh where Gilda Gray had our debut at the original Vickillain Jazz Band at Follies-Berger New York City

22.t: How the word spread, and Japan's 1919 jazz club
22.s: He says records, not the word, spread jazz worldwide, noting a jazz club in Japan in 1919 and New Orleans only in 1949.
22.ch: The word jazz and the band's New York success
22.q: No, not that fast. Yeah. No, it didn't caught on that fast. It was the records that had worldwide distribution that went as far as Honolulu, Germany, Japan. If you look up my clippings, you'll find they had a jazz club in Japan in 1919. Look, they only got a jazz club in New Orleans in 1949. That's…

22.t: Dr. Sushan's 1949 letter about the Hammersmith Palais anniversary
22.s: A December 1949 letter from Dr. Edmond Souchon conveys Lord Donegal's invitation to a London celebration and says only one ODJB started it all.
22.ch: Jazz club letters and Dr. Sushan

22.t: Savoy Peace Ball in London, Marble Arch, and buying out Emil Christian
22.s: La Rocca recalls the band playing the Peace Victory Ball at the Savoy before royalty and the reception for the NC4 flyers, then returning to America and buying out Emil Christian's share so he could go back to England.
22.ch: London and return to New York
22.q: I forgot certain incidents at places like we played in London before we came back to America. We were asked by the British government to play at the Savoy Hotel. That was a celebration of the Peace Victory Ball. Yeah we worked to play the dance music and we went on over there after they had all the…

22.t: Reisenweber's return and sailing to England
22.s: He gives dates for the band's return, last jobs and arrival in England.
22.q: You can prove that from the Army record. I told you we opened it back in Riserwebers around September the 6th. And we played up there. Our contact expired around December the 18th. We were held over, I think, four weeks more until our sailing date. In conjunction with shows, we played around New…

22.t: The London show, the dog-band reviews and the Dixie Club
22.s: He describes critics' mockery, the troops' response, the Dixie Club contract and his return to New York in 1920.
22.q: We played the show. Before we played the show, we rehearsed in the show. When all the Englishmen laughed at us, the papers carried reports that we was a dog band. Some of them said we was yelping hounds. And they didn't describe our music with anything but was no good. That's the critics in London.…

706.t: European musicians and jazz as an international language
706.s: Asked if Europeans look to America, Armstrong says musicians everywhere play the same music, and foreign arrangers wrote for the big bands.
706.q: style of their own well you don't look at it from that they look to America American musicians they're all they got the little something from somewheres and it all sounded good when they played it good and if you go to Japan the musicians play good jazz and if you go to Egypt or down South America…

706.t: European audiences, Belgian friend Robert Goffin, and Caracas telegram album
706.s: Armstrong says audiences warm to the theme song, mentions his Belgian lawyer friend who wrote on jazz and visited him backstage during the war, and describes the scrapbook of telegrams from Caracas.
706.q: The audience is going to enjoy you and things. The people there come there to hear what we're going to do. And from the moment we hit pale moon shining, you know the theme song, everybody sits right there and relax. And from that first note on, the warmth is there. Yeah. Right there in your…

706.t: Feeling at home with audiences around the world
706.s: A student asks how it feels to draw audiences everywhere; Armstrong says he thinks of himself as a neighborhood boy and first went to Sweden in 1934.
706.q: And all you think about New York, I get back off the ship or something, you know? When you say, well it is, and I relax, and that's from the first time I went there in Sweden, 1934. Uh-huh. It's a long time.

706.t: Being an ambassador abroad and playing for audiences
706.s: He says he just plays music, not politics, and tells how he greets French audiences and uses small touches in performance.
706.q: Yeah. I tell them, but it's got to be music when they come to the ambassador and things. Because I don't know about politics. You don't care. I just won't blow the horn. So I have them to understand that, which is kicks and coming out with these cutaways and then play one of them old lowdown blues.…

706.t: His tours of Europe starting in 1932
706.s: He counts eight or ten European trips, first in 1932, staying over a year, returning in 1935.
706.q: Oh, I've been going along about eight or ten times in different times. It was jazz festivals and things. You went over in 32 the first time. First time, 32. Then I would come back, and I went back and stayed over a year or so, and come back in 35. And then from then on, we was going over for…

706.t: Jazz in Japan and its recording industry
706.s: He praises Japanese jazz records and musicians, a nightclub act, and a thriving record business.
706.q: Been to Japan. Oh, that's so great. And I mean, like we say, we don't know who's imitating who. Because everywhere you go, somebody has a little idea of something you did. Or you look at them, something they're doing. And I got jazz records from the Japanese musicians. You don't know whether that…

706.t: Russia trip that fell through and returning America's kindness
706.s: He says he was slated to go to Russia with Ed Sullivan but missed it, will go anywhere Joe Glaser sends him, and feels he owes America.
706.q: You've been over there in Russia? I've been to Russia, yeah. I was slated to go to Russia with Ed Sullivan the week we played in Spileto. But I ate too much spaghetti one night and I'd stay there a week. You're going to go to Russia? I'll go anywhere. Just do it. Anywhere Joe Glazer sent me. I'll…

328.t: Playing in Europe and radio bands
328.s: He played with Dexter Gordon, Johnny Griffin, Kenny Clarke and European radio bands, subsidized for jazz, and was treated very well.
328.q: Sometimes with American musicians, sometime with European musicians. I played with Dexter Gordon, Johnny Griffin, Benny Bailey, oh just a host of guys that were living — Kenny Clarke. All the guys that were living over there and also with the European musicians. We made radio shows. Because see in…

328.s: Europeans live for art; he thinks the US is improving, citing applause at Mostly Mozart.
328.q: Whether they appreciate it more because of that. No their appreciation for jazz is just like their appreciation for all art forms. They live for art. This is so important for them, to go to a concert. They will pass up a meal to go to a concert. They’ve been developed that over many years, that…

328.t: Impact of American expatriates on Europe
328.s: European musicians learned nightly from elite Americans.
328.ch: Europe years and the return home
328.q: The impact that it had overseas in Europe was, a lot of the times the European musicians felt it was unfair for them to have to try to compare to an ensemble like the one I was telling you about. But by the same token, they were going to the club every night, listening to these guys and learning…

328.t: Effect of expatriates' absence on America; few trombonists
328.s: On return he found few trombone players, and the absence of great players hurt American music.
328.ch: Europe years and the return home
328.q: Sure. One of the things that was very apparent was, when I came back in ’77, I would go to a school to work with one of the jazz ensembles, and they had one trombone and seven trumpets, seven saxophones. There wasn’t any trombone players, because in the commercial music that had dominated the scene…

328.s: He wrote for the Brussels Philharmonic and others, learning rehearsal discipline from string players.
328.ch: Europe years and the return home
328.q: Brussels Philharmonic Orchestra. I wrote a big piece for them. I wrote something for one of the classical orchestras in Holland, and I wrote a radio production for one of the string ensembles in Germany, I remember. That was very interesting, because my inexperience there made me write things that…

328.t: Returning for Dexter Gordon's Sophisticated Giant
328.s: Dexter asked him to return for the album; he admires Dexter and criticizes his own arranging.
328.q: Well after I stayed over there for a while then I was asked to come back to do this CD with Dexter Gordon. The “Sophisticated Giant” CD.

328.t: The Joe Haider band with Dexter Gordon
328.s: Co-leading Joe Haider's band, including Dexter and Johnny Griffin, and the album Give Me a Double.
328.ch: Europe years and the return home
328.q: That band, Joe Haider, we were co-leaders. Joe was the one that organized it as far as the music was – I mean, as far as the money was concerned, because in Germany and those places, they had a lot of people that supported projects, especially of new music. If you say you’re going to do a new music…

111.t: Records for J.J. Johnson and the boat to Europe
111.s: J.J. recorded 'J is for Jazz' at Columbia before the tour, and Elvin enjoyed sailing on the S.S. Stockholm.
111.ch: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
111.q: Oh I’d say almost a year. It was a long time. And I left to go with J.J in the latter part of 1957 in the summers. We went to Sweden and we went to Denmark- we were in Scandinavia. We made a record recording—before we went we made these records at Colombia Studios 32nd street: “J is for Jazz” and…

111.t: Scandinavian tour with J.J.: 50,000 in Stockholm
111.s: The tour began in Copenhagen, drew 50,000 to the Kungstradgarden in Stockholm, and lasted three months from Lapland to Gothenburg.
111.ch: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
111.q: Well it started in Copenhagen. We played at this place called “The Three Crowns Hotel Auditorium”. We were there for a couple of days and we went to Stockholm. There we played in the Kungsträdgården and there were over 50,000 people there!

111.t: First European tour with Coltrane: the shopping-bag luggage
111.s: He recalls going to Europe with Trane with dirty shirts and a shopping bag instead of a suitcase.
111.q: I don’t really remember much about it. The only thing that sticks with me is when we go on the stage and play. The rest of it I don’t pay that much attention to. I know I didn’t have a suitcase. I had this beat up tuxedo and these shirts. All of them were dirty. I couldn’t find a place to get my…

111.t: European audiences and treatment compared with the US
111.s: He says no crowd matched J.J.'s 50,000, praises subsidized European clubs, and contrasts the hospitality with the US.
111.q: No I never saw that many. But we went to Scandinavia. We played in Norway and Finland and so there were tremendous audiences. But it never came to the…but I never saw anybody more than when I was with J.J. and I think that’s because the King’s Garden was a very special place for people to go. And…

111.t: Olatunji, and Elvin's own trip to Guinea and Senegal
