72.s: Welburn lists the sessions; Hugues Panassie sent for them and Claude Bolling mimicked many pianists.
72.q: And he spoke very good English. He spoke French. He could talk to us, talk to the band in English. And Mezzrow could transport [sic] all we didn't understand... Mezzrow would transport [sic] it, you know, from him to us.

72.t: Mezzrow, Sammy Price's tour and Paris pay
72.s: Mezzrow was well connected but weak on clarinet; Moore later toured with Sammy Price; he earned $400 a week plus expenses.
72.q: It was around '55, something like that. Maybe it was before '55... I was working at the Jazz Limited in Chicago, and they let me off to go out to make this tour, said he'd have the job open for me when I came back. I went over with Sammy Price. We made the same, about the same tour -- in Paris,…

505.t: First trip to Europe and Lars Werner's record in Stockholm
505.s: At 20 he travelled with $1,000, met Dave Holland in London, and learned of Coltrane's death while recording his first record with Lars Werner in Sweden.
505.q: First trip to Europe. My parents gave me $1,000 and said, go east, young man, with a book called Europe on $5 a Day, if you remember that series. Then it became $10 a day. Student hostels. I went with a tenor. Landed in London. Had a couple names. Called, got Dave Holland on the phone. I said, “I’m…

505.t: IASJ membership and European funding cuts
505.s: The IASJ has about 40 countries but European budget cuts are costing members and may affect a meeting in Ireland.
505.ch: The IASJ and a career in education
505.q: We’re 40 countries, maybe 50, 60 schools. But they drop in and drop out. Now, with funding problems, we’re having a little gap. When IAJE went under a couple years ago, we had 10 new members, like that. Now we’re starting to lose, because guys can’t get $400, euro, 300 euro, I think it’s 400 euro.…

505.t: Tom Harrell's Sail Away and European guest-artist dates
505.s: He recalls Harrell's record and says guest dates in Europe such as one with Franco D'Andrea revived his career.
505.q: That’s a known record. People remember that. That tune, people did. In fact, Lydia did it in some chorus somewhere.

505.t: Jens Winther's piece from the IASJ Baltic cruise of 1996
505.s: The IASJ toured ten Baltic countries by boat, and the piece Winther wrote was rehearsed aboard for the Rhythmic Conservatory opening.
505.q: This is from the IASJ, Baltic cruise, 1996. We went around the Baltic to 10 countries, on the boat, playing jam sessions. He wrote a piece. That was the opening of the Danish Rhythmic Conservatory, done at the end of the tour.

505.t: Working mostly in Europe and the missing middle tier in America
505.s: Eighty to ninety percent of his work is in Europe; he explains American jazz income as A-level or nothing and cites Joe Henderson's revival.
505.ch: The IASJ and a career in education
505.q: He said, “We’re on it,” back and forth with e-mail. He said we don’t have to worry about it. “Yeah, but by the time we’re in Sao Paolo, you’ve got to give me a yes or no.” We got to know two years in advance. Anyway, that’s been very, very interesting and broadening, and of course there’s a real…

374.s: Bosse Broberg of Swedish Radio recorded everything he wrote and funded his projects, including Listen to the Silence for Norwegian Radio.
374.q: I was well received. I stayed a long time. A man named Bosse Broberg was the head of the jazz system of the time. He took care of all the jazz music. He just took his hat off. They recorded everything I ever did.

374.t: The Norwegian mountain ledge that inspired Trip to Pillarguri
374.s: In Norway a host led him sideways along a ledge above an 1800-foot drop; Russell turned back and later wrote a tune about it.
374.q: I’ll just use one. I know it was on – there was a festival in Norway. I don’t know whether they still have it, Norwegian jazz festival. It comes out of Oslo, but the festival site is up into a more mountainous and very dramatic side of Norway, very beautiful, just clear water and . . .

374.t: Guest conducting European radio orchestras and feeling valued
374.s: Daughtry marvels that an unknown American conducted radio orchestras across Scandinavia and Europe; Russell says it was the first time he felt accounted for.
374.q: It was. It was an exciting time and an exciting environment, being in an environment that’s really, first of all, safe, and multiply evolved, because they’re old, go back a long way.

374.t: 1980s recordings and the International Living Time Orchestra
374.s: Daughtry lists 1980s albums, Russell says he does not look back, and he describes touring with British and American players for the British Council.
374.ch: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
374.q: Good players, the Brits. No problems in terms of psychological moods or anything. They’re totally cooperative. Played their heads off. Still do. And a nice group of people. I have been out at times when the psychological makeup of one or two people was very unpleasant. Bandleaders know about that.…

374.t: Conducting with Stockhausen for Danish radio
374.s: His sextet played at the Tivoli between two orchestras performing Stockhausen, and he became friends with the composer.
374.ch: European recordings and return to America
374.q: Did a concert with a very modern composer – the modern composer at the time. I shouldn’t start this at this time in the morning.

509.t: Receptive audiences at the North Sea, in Paris and in Japan
509.s: She describes the thunderous applause in Europe, the respect of Japanese audiences, and watching Murder, She Wrote in Japan.
509.q: Child, mm, mm, mm, I could go on for days. I didn‘t know what a receptive audience was until I did . . . the first stop was at the North Sea. And I didn‘t realize how many people were in this huge place until I was on the stage and way in the back somebody opened a door, and then I saw a glimpse of…

509.t: Why European and Japanese audiences respect jazz, the Dutch boy and the fan club
509.s: She says Europeans study jazz in school, recalling a Dutch boy who knew Coltrane and a Japanese fan club.
509.q: Well, see, one thing they do . . . I think the answer to that question is that most children are coming up, especially the jazz enthusiasts, they‘re hearing these American jazz artists, right, and they studied it in school, right? So right away, you know . . . I mean, I doubt seriously if they are…

509.s: Japan calmed her with its politeness and precise timing; returning to JFK felt rough.
509.q: I said, ―Just something is missing, you know what I mean?‖ I said, ―I haven‘t heard m.f. or f___ you. I haven‘t heard any of those things. It‘s almost two weeks. It‘s odd.‖ And we both laughed, and it was the truth. I mean, it really helped us. We got off the plane, got off in JFK, first thing we…

509.t: The jazz press in the United States and in France
509.s: She says most American writers copy other articles, while the French press has treated her well.
509.q: A few writers that know what they‘re writing about, that I respect. But the majority of them will look at your bio, or look at another article, and take from that. I think a writer should go . . . if the situation were reversed, I would go and listen to the artist and then write about the artist,…

509.t: Earning more per concert in France and Japan
509.s: She makes more abroad, getting twice as much for one concert and about 75 percent more overall.
509.q: Well, let‘s see. When I was doing those three years, we were everywhere but home. I made a lot more money. Well, it‘s especially good right now in . . . okay, I‘m sorry. Since I‘m well known in France, I make a lot of money in France and Japan, and you don‘t have to work yourself to death. Like you…

406.t: Europe with Sammy Price in 1958, cancelled when the Pope died
406.s: He went to Paris and Holland with Sammy Price, Doc Cheatham and J. C. Higginbotham. The tour was cancelled when the Pope died, and he flew home.
406.ch: Streetcar, Cab revival shows and trips abroad
406.q: This was after the show, because we went to Europe in '58 with Sam, and then we came back and took another show -- another show down in Miami that year, in '58 too, which didn't last very long, with Cab Calloway.

406.t: State Department tour of Africa with Dick Vance's group, 1969
406.s: The four-piece group accompanied the American Dance Theater with Mama Lou Parks's dancers through nine countries and 22 cities, and a documentary was made.
406.q: Well, when I went to Africa, I went to Africa with -- it was Dick Vance's group. And we went -- we had four pieces, and we went there to play the American Dance Theater. We had Avon Long and Cookan Brown and Gib Gibson and the Park Dancers, you know, Mrs. Park.

406.t: Saints and Sinners in Europe, 1969: London cancelled, Copenhagen memorial
406.s: The tour with Red Richards, Buddy Tate and Herman Autrey was not needed in London, so they flew to Copenhagen for a memorial to Timme Rosenkrantz.
406.q: And after coming back from Africa I -- that next year I took a trip, in 1969 I took a trip with Red Richards, Saints and Sinners, back to Europe again, and we had Buddy Tate and Herman Autrey.

406.t: Bus tour through Spain and France
406.s: The group flew to Barcelona and then did one-nighters by bus through France to Paris and Belgium, seeing the countryside.
406.q: But any -- we went on, left there, and we went down to -- no, I think we played Zurich. Then we went from Zurich down to Barcelona. We flew down to Barcelona. And then after we played Barcelona, we took a bus and came all -- it was a wonderful trip. We came by bus. It was one nighters all up…

406.t: The Jazz Train show in Italy, Germany and Switzerland, 1960
406.s: He conducted the Jazz Train, a revue of jazz history with Leslie Scott and about forty people, through Italy and Germany with Tommy Benford on drums. He left in Switzerland when the pay went to percentage.
406.ch: Streetcar, Cab revival shows and trips abroad
406.q: That was a show made up from -- well, it was -- Jazz Train was the history, supposed to be a history of American jazz with theater, and we did things like Porgy and Bess and -- and it was a nice show. We had Leslie Scott. He was the star. And Ura Lee Unitas -- I forgot her -- she was, you know, a…

229.t: Barry Martyn forms the old timers band
229.s: Drummer Barry Martyn recruits him, with Montudie Garland and Joe Darensbourg, for an old-timers band that rehearses through 1973.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: While we were there this drummer, English drummer from English came in and asked me if I wanted to join his band because he wanted to organize an old timers band to travel.

229.s: He says he has been to Europe about twenty times, five times in 1978, and was known there from old records.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: Yes they did. Barry said that one of the reasons that he wanted me was that the people over there know you, they heard your records and know about you.

229.s: The February tour is marred by illness, with Joe Darensbourg sent home from London, and the band stays in cheap hotels.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: Very good. We didn't got to Europe until the next year, February, and this was in September when we made the New England tour and we came back home. In February, we also made a partial tour of the states and

229.t: The first Legends tour and recording in Minneapolis
229.s: The band rehearses and tours from Chicago through a Wisconsin ski lodge to Minneapolis, where they make their first record.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: Well we started rehearsing a couple of months later; this was near the holidays of '72, around December, and we started rehearsing the next year, around February or March, around in there. We rehearsed up to our next tour

229.t: A single French concert and Eastern Airlines routing
229.s: He recalls one trip to France for one concert and the manager booking only Eastern Airlines.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: He had something to do with Eastern Airlines, and so he tried to make all our travels on Eastern Airline. Everytime we go to New York from Los Angeles we had to go by way of Atlanta instead of direct.

88.t: South America 1960: Caracas, Rio and Buenos Aires musicians
88.s: Touring South America with a 20-piece book, Lee found the Buenos Aires players excellent, Rio's strings great and horns terrible.
88.q: So we did that thing, and then we went to South America in 1960, and that was an experience that I think musicians should have because -- they say music is an international language, and it is -- and that's when you find out that it is. Because our first stop was in Caracas, Venezuela, and from…

88.t: The Japanese tour: hip audiences and copyist bands
88.s: On the Orient trip Nat's love songs brought the house down, and Japanese bands copied Miller, Goodman and Herman perfectly.
88.q: Yeah, it was always Buddy Cole who would always play the things on ... that was when we went to the Orient, it was quite a good experience; we did an hour and a half television show there, and it's funny how the language, you know, with music, language is no barrier. They just -- in Japan, they…

88.s: Lee compares Mexico City and Uruguay musicians and says recordings are leveling quality everywhere.
88.q: Oh, in Mexico City, the musicians were very good. They were very good -- especially like, I was talking about then, but since I've been in the record business, I went to Mexico to record, and you don't find any difference. Especially the way music is today, everybody is listening to records, and…

88.t: Manila: the promoter's cars and the weak musicians
88.s: In Manila the promoter provided each member's make of car, and the local musicians were poor compared with Japan.
88.q: On the trip to the Orient, we came back through -- we came to Manila and we played a large stadium in Manila; the man that owns it and the promoter, his name was, let's see, Arnetta -- he was supposed to be the wealthiest man in Manila. Now when he brings an act in, he finds out what type of…

88.t: The 1954 London Palladium exchange with Ted Heath
88.s: The Palladium initially refused Lee's trio members, leading to a reciprocal exchange in which Ted Heath's band toured the States.
88.q: Yes ... yeah. So we were -- this was in '54, and then after we came over, I think the next group was Stan Kenton, and they started exchanging, but Ted Heath even traveled with us, with June Christie and the comedian that married Lucille Ball -- that was the comic with us --

409.t: English fans who knew every record
409.s: In England fans had all their records and knew all the details, while American audiences did not.
409.q: Oh, yeah. I never will forget that. Because when we got off the boat, and when we got to the hotel and went out, everybody knew you. The same as in America. They knew you better than the people did in America. And they would invite you to their home, and they had all your records. Knew what to talk…

409.t: Jazz audiences in Europe versus America
409.s: Cootie says Europe is educated about jazz and America is not, blaming disc jockeys; jazz courses only started seven years earlier.
409.q: See, on jazz, the people in Europe, they're very well educated on jazz, which the American public are not. Any place you go in Europe, the general public are very much educated. On jazz music. That's something that we don't have here in America.

409.t: Ellington's works and tours from 1963: My People, Near East, Far East
409.s: Dance prompts the 1963-64 tours and the Far East Suite.
409.q: Yeah. I remember all those things.

409.t: The 1968 South America tour and the 1969 White House party
409.s: The band was mobbed in South America and Wild Bill joined in 1969.
409.q: I think he filled a role what Duke had in mind.

409.t: The royal party and the Prince on Sonny's drums
409.s: At a millionaire's party a royal prince played Sonny Greer's drums, and the band was received warmly.
409.q: Yeah. He got on Sonny's drums and beat the drums at the party that night.

147.t: Cities played and no segregation in Europe
147.s: Crawford lists Scandinavia and London on the tour and says the band met no segregation and stayed in good white hotels.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: Stayed at white hotels, yes, not maybe the best, but they were good, because Lunsford, they wouldn't let us, as a matter of fact, no, we had to stay in a good hotel. Yeah, Lunsford was a wonderful gentleman.

147.t: European audiences, dancing and women, and constant touring at home
147.s: Audiences in Europe reacted as in America to the band's book, and Crawford says the band toured every whistle stop at home.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: No. No, they didn't, even in the Scandinavian countries, where they perhaps are used to doing the polka and all those kind of dances, we played just what we went there to play, and we played it, and we went over quite well.

147.t: Italy, Scandinavia and London on the European trip
147.s: Crawford says the band toured Scandinavia, went down to Italy and visited London, where he heard imitations of American music.
147.ch: Precision, the union and learning to read
147.q: Italy. First we went to Scandinavia -- Stockholm, Norway, Sweden, all the important cities there, that could afford to hear this band. I'm very proud of that band.

147.t: The 1937 Europe tour arranged by Harold Oxley
147.s: Crawford says Oxley arranged the 1937 tour and recalls slipping away from Oxley's family for a night out with Al Norris.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: And Al Norrissee and myself, naturally, whiskey heads, we got up out of bed, not out of bed, maybe out of bed or out of our room in Oslo or either in Stockholm, and we were going out, just go out on the town a little bit.

147.t: Ship's officers befriend Crawford on the way to Europe
147.s: Crawford recalls Polish ship officers gathering around him and asking about America.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: Well, all I remember is for some reason most all people were just crazy about me. I don't know whether it was my personality. Wasn't my drumming. And so even on the boat, M. S. [Polish boat Pretori] the officers would gather around me --

385.t: Paris as home base; recording in Europe
385.s: He lived near the Champs-Elysees, met Mickey Baker and Kenny Clarke, and found European studios poor.
385.q: Well, home base was Paris. And would make our little trips and we would meet back there, and then he'd plan some more. But the home base was Paris. I used to live approximately three blocks from the Champs-Elysees. I met a few fellas over there -- Mickey Baker, he's been over there, he's really…

385.t: European sidemen; practicing with records and tapes
385.s: Players from France and Afghanistan swung, and he practices with records and tapes.
385.q: Yeah, we had a couple of guys. Let's see, one was from France -- a bass player, and then they have another guy from Afghanistan. They couldn't speak no English, but they could play.

385.t: Spain tours and the 1971 Town Hall guitar concert
385.s: He recalls concerts in Spain and the Town Hall guitar concert, where he was the only black guitarist and recorded in one day.
385.q: Oh, the album, yeah that was really tough on me. Yep. Well, all those heavy guys, you know, and they included me-- I'm the only black guy in there. George Benson was on there but I... his company wouldn't let him release somethin'-- anyhow he didn't get any PR at all. But he was on the program, he…

385.s: He played with John Letterman and Wallace Bishop, who he says played as if in 1930.
385.q: ...He never did progress, as you might say. Boy, he played like he was playin' in 1930. I shouldn't say that...

385.t: The 1968 European tour with Milt Buckner
385.s: The tour was arranged through Arvell Shaw and George Wein with Buddy Tate and Cozy Cole; he found European audiences quiet.
385.q: Oh, it was good. Milt is one of the finest guys that can take any kind of thing and laugh it off. He used to -- amaze me -- he would laugh if you dropped a pencil on the floor. He was a fun cat. I don't care what you do -- you could say, hey man, look at that bird flying by and he would break out…

168.t: First trip to Europe as first recalled, with Norman Granz
168.s: Stewart first places his European debut in the mid-'50s on a Granz package with Erroll Garner, and says he was treated royally.
168.q: If I'm not mistaken, I think it was around the mid-'50s, yes, and I think it was a Norman Granz thing. And it so happened that Erroll Garner was on the package. He wasn't playing with me, but he was along with the group when -- that was my first time to go to Europe.

168.t: European tours and recordings with Milt Buckner, Jo Jones and others
168.s: He toured England, Spain, Italy and Germany with Buckner and Jones, and recorded since 1972 with Big Joe Turner, Wild Bill Davis, Al Casey and others.
168.q: Milt Buckner, that's right, and of course, I've toured quite a few places, many places. I've been many places in England.

168.t: Django Reinhardt and whether they met
168.s: He thinks he met Reinhardt in 1948 but never played with him.
168.q: I may have. You know, the difference -- the length of time in the years? That goes back quite a ways.

168.t: Touring Australia and its rugby league clubs
168.s: In Australia they played rugby league clubs between Sydney and Melbourne, sat in with local musicians, and saw koalas and kangaroos.
168.ch: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
168.q: If I can remember, when we arrived in Australia, we -- it was Sidney, I believe it was -- and we toured quite a bit. We played places which they call -- you know the game that they have in Australia was called rugby --

168.t: Correcting the first Europe trip: Paris festival in 1948 with Panassie
168.s: Stewart realizes his first European trip was the 1948 Paris festival organized by Panassie, with Garner, Bechet, Parker and Miles Davis, before the later England trip.
168.q: I suddenly remembered that we went in 1948 and that wasn't with Norman Granz. That was [Hugues] Pannassie, his last name was.

30.t: First European trip with Ellington in 1933
30.s: Europe with Duke in 1933 or 1934 was a thrill; they played only two shows at the London Palladium and ducked the crowds at the stage door.
30.q: Oh, that's quite a thrill. We played that -- what's that theater over there? We only played two shows -- one show -- two shows, yeah, in England, in London.

30.t: Missing this summer's European tour after his operation
30.s: He missed two European dates this year after his operation, including the Nice festival with George Wein, and Benny Carter went in his place.
30.q: Yeah. I missed two this year on account of my operation. I didn't want to take any chances because if I had gotten sick over there, that would have been terrible. Somebody would be talking a language I wouldn't even know what they're saying or whatever.

30.t: Crossing the Atlantic with Ellington: Braud's storm and toupee
30.s: He likes sea travel; Braud blamed Bigard for talking up a storm when the ship showed a movie called Storm at Daybreak, and later threw his London toupee into the ocean.
30.q: Yeah, well, we only gave a concert, and when we gave the concert we had the boat for ourselves then, you know, because we went tourist and when you're going tourist

30.t: African cities, American-style music and coconut drying
30.s: They toured all over Africa; the cities were modern, local bands tried to play American music while tribal drumming was separate, and he saw green coconuts laid out in the sun beside ships waiting to load.
30.q: Yeah, we went all over Africa. Abidjan [Kenya, Ivory Coast, Ghana] and all them places. I can't think of all them funny names.

30.t: Recording in France and England; the later session with Claude Luter
30.s: Bigard has been to France several times and recorded in France and England only with Louie and Duke until Mrs. Bigard recalls a later record with Claude Luter around 1960.
30.q: With whom? I've recorded with Louie, with Duke -- and recorded in England with Duke. I never recorded with no Frenchman.

238.t: Why English audiences knew her and her decision to tour Britain
238.s: Her records reached England via a German forces radio disc jockey, and after hesitating she accepted Gastel's bookings for two tours.
238.ch: England, later career and closing thoughts
238.q: Oh, yes, he did, definitely. Yes, he did. As a matter of fact, I went twice, I think in one year, and it was just a tremendous success, really.

238.t: British tour: sidemen, Jack Jackson and the Scottish response
238.s: She took Earl Hyde and George Duvivier, toured with Jack Jackson and found fans in Scotland who knew all her songs.
238.ch: England, later career and closing thoughts
238.q: I had -- when I first went I took Earl Hyde on drums, and George Duvivier, who's today one of the greatest and one of the finest bass players around, amongst the finest. They went with me the first time, and the second time, for that matter. And it was just tremendous, really. The response was so…

238.t: Variety houses, Lew Grade's circle and fan Alan Hobbs
238.s: She played a week at a time plus Sunday variety shows in London, met the Grade brothers and agent Mumford, and a young fan Alan Hobbs followed her tour.
238.ch: England, later career and closing thoughts
238.q: Now, what I'd do, I'd work six days in one place and on Sundays we'd come to London and do -- I think they called it variety. They called it variety there. I think that's the name they called it, variety. Variety houses and variety concerts. But it was really variety, because you know

238.s: A Brazilian poet and director who has all her records befriended her when his group visited, and urges her to tour South America.
238.ch: England, later career and closing thoughts
238.q: Well, I'm going to say this briefly. Well, this young fellow is a poet and he's a director and he's -- well, he's into music. He played guitar at one time. And his name is Emilio Bele de Cavajo, and he is quite busy, from South America. He's in Rio de Janeiro. And he was here with a show. Let me…

238.t: Foreign offers, the cost of touring and working by feeling
238.s: She would tour Europe again only with records out, prefers her own sympathetic musicians such as Morris Edwards and George Duvivier, and plays by feeling.
238.ch: England, later career and closing thoughts
238.q: I got a letter just a few weeks ago from somebody wanting to get -- bring me -- from a Scandinavian booking agent. And I've gotten calls within the last year from people wanting me to go into Europe, you know. But my feeling now is that I would like to do something like that, if I have something…

473.t: Closing the bill at the Olympia in a four-hour music-hall show
473.s: At the Olympia he followed circus acts with horses to close the bill with "Struttin' with Some Barbecue" and won good reviews; Sidney Bechet followed him, and Delaunay sent him on to Belgium.
473.q: I laid off a week and he paid me just the same. Then the next two weeks I worked at the Olympic Theater there, downtown, Boulevard des Capucines. And I went in there, and this was something I'd never seen before. All kinds of acts, the show going on for hours, horses and everything on the stage.…

473.t: Grappelli's film records, Sugar Ray Robinson's entourage, and francs to Belgium
473.s: He recorded for a Grappelli film that was shot after he left; in Paris he took June Clark to dinner and found a way to send francs to Belgium and then home.
473.q: Stephane Grappelli was nice. I had another week off which, after the two weeks I did there. That was really finishing all that he had promised me, the four weeks. I had another week off. Stephane Grappelli got a picture together. He got a picture and he got me in there to make the records. We made…

473.t: Ten weeks in Belgium and run-ins with King Farouk over beer
473.s: At the coast resort he refused champagne offered by King Farouk, who also phoned him at ten a.m. to join him at his cabana; locals held Jonah Jones parties and asked about Jackie Robinson and segregation.
473.q: But all the records I did over there, and when I got paid, I just sent it to Belgium because I was going there anyway, so I did that. And when we got to Belgium, we stayed there 10 weeks. It was nice, beautiful. With this same band, Andre Rialte, and Guy Leon was playing the trumpet, and we had a…

473.t: Delaunay brings him to Paris for the Salle Pleyel festival, Panassie objecting
473.s: Charles Delaunay invited him over while Hugues Panassie advised against; Jones had been Panassie's favourite since Louis the Second days, and got four weeks guaranteed, playing the festival at Salle Pleyel.
473.q: Yeah, uh-huh. He called me back many a time for another show, you know, but then I was doing something else, because after that closed, then Delaunay [Charles] was writing to me all the time about come over, and [Hugues] Panassie was saying don't come. Because Panassie was supposed to be my boy.…

473.t: Refusing cut-rate offers and the Porgy and Bess stage solo pay dispute
473.s: Porgy and Bess producers offered to hire him again at his old salary, and he had earlier bargained from $25 to $75 extra to play Howard Roberts's stage trumpet spot; Delaunay told him to go home rather than work cheaply.
473.q: So I could have stayed over much longer, you know, because the show was coming back to Europe, and they wanted somebody that knew the show to play it, and they wouldn't have to worry, you know, about nothing.

769.s: They leave in December 1958 and reach Liverpool and London, meeting Ken Collier's brass band at the station; Sweden and Denmark follow.
769.q: I think it was Cavalier. Yeah, I'm more than sure it was Cavalier. Because we had Tom Jefferson on trumpet at that time. Well, anyway, after we got through playing in Frisco, where we came on back home, where Elton, he stopped off in Los Angeles, so he was going to make up his mind to stay there.…

769.s: Asked to go to Japan, he tours three months with Lewis's group, is in Tokyo the day the president is assassinated, and returns in December 1963.
769.q: Yeah. And George, yeah. That's right. Yeah, that was the All-Stars that played then. And, uh... Well, first thing, next thing came up was Japan. Yes. Jeff asked him, said, Joe, you'd like to go to Japan? I said, yeah, what is Spain? He told me.

769.t: Plans for a tour and clearing up the 1959 band lineup

813.t: Jazz appreciation in Europe and expatriate musicians

448.t: Why America undervalues jazz compared with Europe
448.s: America sees culture as European and jazz as not respectable; Europeans valued it as uniquely American.

448.t: Bechet's view of his place in jazz and his success in France

843.t: Growing crowds and visitors from around the world

Oh yes, and, uh, also we've noticed that we're getting a steady clientele of people, uh, people that are living in the city, that are coming back, and people from out of town who have heard by word of mouth. It's growing. We have... Yes.…

And I know there is a tremendous trend toward Dixieland music in Italy. They like it. They really love it. In fact, they have a lot…

885.t: Dupree's rhythm and meeting him again at Montreux
885.s: Whether Dupree influenced his drumming, and meeting him by surprise in Switzerland years later.
885.q: Yeah, just, not necessarily drumming. I just, whatever you would play, I knew a back beat would fit into it, you know. I can't recall all of the tunes I have, some of the tapes that he even sent me.

300.s: Humphrey describes performing at the Olympics cultural program in Mexico City.
300.q: about the most riding band? Yeah. In Mexico, we played a different corks. It's, uh, oh, it's a big park band. They claim it's seven wide, seven miles long. Beautiful place. We played a different section about three times at the, you know, different sections of that park, outdoors. And we played in…

392.t: Preservation Hall, Japan tours and musicians abroad

392.q: I don't know too much about them, Tom, but I do believe that some of the regular, some of the die-hard Vixeland fans do frequent those places. But then too, I think that just a lot of visitors drop in. And whether, what degree, what varying degrees they like music, whether it's just curiosity many…

189.t: Frog on trombone, Bob Martin's accent, and keeping the tradition

177.t: English revival bands and King Colyer
177.s: Jiles thinks Ken Colyer played closest to old Dixieland and that Chris Barber's band skipped around when playing a rag.
177.q: Well I think King Collier to me, not because I made the record with him, but I think he played more near to the old Dixieland and these guys that he was playing with. What I can recall, to one of the numbers that this Englishman played, one of the rags that they tried to play and I couldn't catch…

770.t: Brubeck, Marian Anderson and jazz drawing crowds at the Brussels fair
770.s: Jack says jazz made the biggest impact compared with other US acts and drew crowds at Brussels, though the government did not supply it.
770.q: they've had the symphony over there and they've had Marian Anderson they like Marian Anderson very much in fact they spoke of her first when they talk about things that have been sent over

741.q: Some of them do, for sure. I think you take someone like Jan Garbarek and he can play the saxophone in a lot of different ways. But you’re going to hear a very strong Norwegian, folk kind of element in his playing because that’s what he wants to pursue. But there are also a lot of European…

516.t: Nina Simone and musicians living overseas

516.q: Yeah, yeah. It does, it does. And it really comes out of the old spirituals when people were singing and hopes for and prayers for a better day, better conditions. I saw a heart wrenching interview, I mean sometimes stuff just pops up on YouTube and I say, “Oh I’ve just got to hear this,” something…

615.t: Overseas audiences and the aging jazz party crowd
615.s: He finds foreign audiences knowledgeable, worries jazz parties are too costly for young listeners, and describes his Monday bar gig.
615.q: I think it’s accepted very well. You know the main thing that I notice is that in general, overseas, there isn’t such a saturation of media — television — there aren’t ninety channels of T.V. in France or certainly not England and various places like that. So I think people are more used to going…

140.t: Avant garde in Europe versus America today
140.s: Rowe asks about under-represented ends of jazz; Ali says avant garde is popular in Europe and alive but not well in America.
140.q: Well back, like in the 70s, like the early part of the 70s, I don’t know too much about the Dixieland but probably all even Dixieland and avant garde now, but not now, not so much now, because the avant garde is really popular in Europe. And I mean you know we get like huge crowds in Europe with…

533.t: Louis Hayes in Paris with Cannonball: even the kids speak French
533.s: Allen urges Rowe to talk to Louis Hayes, then tells the story of Hayes's first trip to Europe with Cannonball.
533.q: He’s a character. You know, I’ve got to tell you a funny story. This was the first time he went to Europe with Cannonball. They were in Paris. And they’d meet in the lobby for a sound check, and there’s no Louis. And they’re waiting around for Louis. So here he comes, after they’d been waiting…

1001.t: Upcoming England trip and English jazz musicians
1001.s: Five weeks in England, Ronnie Scott's club, and England's long jazz history.
1001.q: Sometimes I take a quartet with me, other times, this particular time I’m not. There are a bunch of wonderful musicians in London, or all around England, who I go over and work with.

200.s: Egyptian audiences respected Sun Ra in 1971; in Germany, Vienna and Russia the band played classics, with a solo for Allen.

434.q: Well yeah, you’re right. The music today, there is a sense in which America still dominates culturally, but it’s not because of great quality anymore, it’s because rock was in or punk rock was in for about a year, or acid rock was in, there are many subdivisions of garbage music. But those truly…

313.t: Armstrong, LPs and the first jazz books

313.q: Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following…

804.t: Touring Japan with James Morrison and Rolf Harris
804.s: Baker recalls the Tokyo expo tour with James Morrison and Rolf Harris, whose watercolours went to charity, and novelty Australian songs.
804.q: Yeah, well, at one time that was true. I remember hearing that on the radio when I was young in the sixties. Rolf Harris. And actually I toured with Rolf Harris once.

673.t: Jazz abroad, Japan, Europe and Cooper's Paris plans

And the people are dead serious about it too. I go to Japan a lot. I have a lot of Japanese friends, musicians. And they are just as…

154.s: A month in Russia and the feeling of a tight road band.
154.q: Yeah. Great. It was a great band. With that band you get the feeling like when you go on the road with a band and you get tight. That only happens on the road. And that month it happened. It was great. But it doesn’t happen too much anymore.

910.t: Touring Japan and playing in a guitar trio

728.t: Dream of Europe and moving abroad in 2000

787.s: He describes flying to Aachen where Ralf Kemper arranged for the symphony and conductor Christopher Ward to perform his Americana Suite, his first time hearing another conductor lead his work.

436.s: Pete describes the warm welcome and knowledgeable fans in Japan and Europe.

158.t: Being treated like an artist in Europe

693.t: Touring Europe and Japan; subsidized jazz in Germany

520.s: Long European tours with his groups, tiring of clubs, and returning this summer for festivals.

720.t: Advice to young writers and European radio bands

640.t: Playing overseas and the economics of touring with pick-up bands

59.t: European versus American appreciation of jazz
59.s: Europeans appreciated jazz as an art form earlier; jazz is now heard more in concert than in clubs.
59.q: Well at that time it was quite noticeable. I’m not sure you could say — I think you could say it’s the same now. 1048.t: Europeans, defining traditional jazz, and Vladivostok
1048.s: Asked to define traditional jazz, Johnson demurs, says Europeans understand it better, and tells of a Vladivostok radio station wanting T-shirts.

542.t: London: studio reputation, Brotherhood of Breath, Nottingham gig

809.t: Touring with Elvin in Europe, South America and the US

335.s: He toured Japan, Europe and New Zealand annually and finds jazz audiences universal.

338.t: Living and playing in Sydney, then returning around 1980

226.t: Learning the touring system and Wes Montgomery's customs story

383.t: Reception abroad in South Africa and Ireland
383.s: Wilson says audiences in South Africa and Ireland were as enthusiastic as anywhere, with music overcoming politics.
383.ch: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
383.q: Oh, as good a reception as I ever had in any part of the world. The enthusiasm of South Africa just like the enthusiasm in Ireland, too. For some reason, the emotional enthusiasm of the jazz fans in Ireland exceeds anything that I have seen -- people kissed my hands like I was a Pope or something.…

93.t: The 1966 George Wein jazz festival tour and the stage names
93.s: In 1966 the tap dancers toured Europe with George Wein's festival, hoping to surprise Chuckles; their stage names were Kind Sir, Good Father, Tap Dancer's Dream and Godfather.
93.q: we came back from a tour with a jazz festival, which was the George Wein, you know. He had a monarchy with the jazz musicians. And he was going to get -- you see, Chuckles was working for this Gezler Gunther over there. See, I think he was working in Paris at that time.

384.t: Lyons Corner House in London and flying to France
384.s: The Specht band played at the Lyons Corner House in London; Morehouse did not play in France, which was just vacation, because the French musicians did not want outsiders.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: Specht, Weems and learning to play
384.q: Because none of the Frenchmen knew us at all. And they didn't want to take a chance on putting a rough guy in there and spoiling their caliber of music.

388.q: I'm gonna touch lightly upon my associations with some more wonderful musicians, and I'd like to get to Pee Wee Irwin -- I say touch lightly upon them because there are so many people to cover. Right now, I'm running out of tape.

427.s: In Paris he played with a big show of old-time American musicians; in Hawaii he drank with a manager's mother.

31.t: Leaving Duke to arrange for Norma Miller's show in Venezuela
31.s: In 1950 Whaley quit Duke over money, wrote the show for Norma Miller and toured Caracas, Maracaibo and Colombia, leaving through Barranquilla.
31.q: With Duke Ellington's band. And I asked him for more money. He said he wasn't going to give me any more money, so I quit. I came back to New York. Al Sears quit the band also that same time I did, and we come back to New York.
